Confucius identified seventy-seven disciples proficient in the six arts, categorizing them by virtue (Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, Zhong Gong), political skill (Ran You, Ji Lu), eloquence (Zaiwo, Zigong), and erudition (Ziyou, Zixia). He noted individual traits: Zhuan Sun was extreme, Zeng Shen slow, Gao Chai stupid, Zhong You rude, and Yan Hui poor. Zigong, rejecting fate, became a successful merchant. Confucius respected figures like Laozi, Zang Boyu, Yan Zhongping, Laolaizi, Zichan, and Meng Gongchuo, and praised others from earlier eras. Yan Hui (Yan Yuan), thirty years younger than Confucius, was praised for virtue, living frugally without changing his joy. Confucius said he restrained himself to conform to etiquette, was not stupid, and shared a philosophy of serving when employed and hiding when not. Yan Hui died prematurely at twenty-nine, causing Confucius great grief. Duke Ai of Lu was told Yan Hui was the best learner, never transferring anger or repeating mistakes.
Min Ziqian, fifteen years younger, was deemed exceptionally filial, avoiding official service. Ran Boniu suffered an incurable disease; Confucius lamented his fate. Zhong Gong, asked about governance, was advised to be courteous and cautious; Confucius deemed him fit for high office despite his humble father. Ran Qiu, twenty-nine years younger, managed military affairs for the Ji family; Confucius encouraged his timidity. Zilu (Zhong You), nine years younger, was bold and straightforward, initially bullying Confucius but later becoming a disciple. Confucius taught him to prioritize righteousness over bravery, and he died in Wei during a rebellion, tying his hat before death.
Zaiwo, eloquent, questioned the three-year mourning period, suggesting one year sufficed; Confucius rebuked him for lacking benevolence. Zaiwo later died in a rebellion in Qi. Zigong, thirty-one years younger, was articulate and wealthy. Confucius compared him to a vessel and praised his humility. Zigong’s diplomatic mission saved Lu, disrupted Qi, destroyed Wu, strengthened Jin, and enabled Yue’s dominance, altering the balance of power among states.
Ziyou, forty-five years younger, governed Wucheng with music and ritual; Confucius joked about using a “knife to kill a chicken” but later praised him. Zixia, forty-four years younger, discussed the Book of Songs with Confucius, who noted his slight deficiency. After Confucius’s death, Zixia taught in Hexi. Zizhang, forty-eight years younger, learned about gaining office through caution and about achieving success through loyalty and respect. Zeng Shen, forty-six years younger, understood filial piety and wrote the Book of Filial Piety.
Other disciples included Tantai Mieming, initially judged poorly by appearance but later renowned; Mi Zijian, praised as a gentleman; Yuan Xian, who valued poverty over shame; Gongye Chang, married to Confucius’s daughter; Nangong Kuo, praised for morality; and Gao Chai, deemed stupid. Youruo, resembling Confucius, was briefly treated as a teacher but failed to answer questions. The text lists thirty-five disciples with recorded ages and deeds, and forty-two without, concluding that later accounts vary, with the author relying on The Analects for accuracy.

The king of Nanyue, Wei Tuo (Zhao Tuo), was from Zhending. During the Qin dynasty, after conquering the six states, the Qin annexed Yang Yue, establishing Guilin, Nanhai, and Xiangjun, and resettled criminals there to live with the Yue people for thirteen years. Zhao Tuo served as the magistrate of Longchuan County in Nanhai. In the second year of the Qin dynasty, Ren Xiao, the captain of Nanhai, fell ill. He summoned Zhao Tuo and explained that with Chen Sheng’s rebellion and the Qin’s cruel policies, the Central Plains were in chaos. He noted that Nanhai was remote and could be defended by mountains and sea, and suggested Zhao Tuo could establish a state. Ren Xiao appointed Zhao Tuo as acting captain. After Ren Xiao’s death, Zhao Tuo cut off roads, gathered troops, killed Qin-appointed officials, and replaced them with his cronies. Following the Qin’s fall, he annexed Guilin and Xiangjun and declared himself King Wu of Nanyue. Emperor Gaozu of Han, due to the people’s exhaustion, spared Zhao Tuo. In the eleventh year of Gaozu, he sent Lu Jia to confirm Zhao Tuo as King of Nanyue, with an agreement for envoys and harmony with Baiyue. During Empress Lü’s reign, officials banned ironware trade with Nanyue. Zhao Tuo suspected King Changsha’s influence, declared himself Emperor Wu of Nanyue, and attacked Changsha’s border cities. Empress Lü sent General Zhou Zao to attack, but heat and illness halted the army. After her death, the Han stopped. Zhao Tuo expanded his territory to over 10,000 miles, bribing Minyue, Xiou, and Luoyue, and acted as an emperor.
In the first year of Emperor Wen of Han, the emperor honored Zhao Tuo’s parents’ tomb and his cousins. He sent Lu Jia to rebuke Zhao Tuo for claiming the emperor title. Zhao Tuo apologized, citing fear of King Changsha and the queen’s actions, and claimed he used the title for self-comfort among barbarians. He pledged vassalage to Han, removed imperial trappings, and continued as a vassal. During Emperor Jing’s era, Zhao Tuo outwardly submitted but secretly kept the emperor title. He died in the fourth year of Jianyuan, succeeded by his grandson Zhao Hu.
Zhao Hu faced an attack from Minyue’s King Ying. He requested Han intervention, and Emperor Wu sent troops, leading to Ying’s death. Zhao Hu thanked the emperor but, advised by ministers, avoided visiting the capital, fearing captivity. He died as King Wen. His son Yingqi, who had married a woman from Handan and fathered Zhao Xing, became king. Yingqi hid his grandfather’s emperor seal, refused to visit the capital due to fear of Han laws, and died as King Ming. Zhao Xing succeeded, with his mother as queen mother.
The queen mother, who had previously committed adultery with Anguo Shaoji, sought to submit to Han. Emperor Wu sent Anguo Shaoji to persuade them. The young king and queen mother agreed to become vassals, but Prime Minister Lu Jia, who had served three kings and held great influence, opposed. He feared losing power and plotted rebellion. At a banquet, the queen mother tried to provoke the Han envoy to kill Lu Jia, but the envoy hesitated. Lu Jia left, gathered troops, and refused to meet the king. The queen mother’s efforts failed.
The emperor sent Han Qianqiu with 2,000 troops to South Vietnam. Lu Jia rebelled, killed the king, queen mother, and Han envoys, and installed Zhao Jiande as king. Han Qianqiu’s army was ambushed and destroyed. The emperor then launched a large-scale attack in the fifth year of Yuanding, with generals Lu Bode, Yang Pu, and others leading forces from multiple directions. In the sixth year, Yang Pu’s troops captured Panyu, and Lu Bode’s forces accepted surrenders. Lu Jia and Zhao Jiande fled by sea but were captured. South Vietnam was pacified, and the Han established nine counties. The kingdom lasted five generations for ninety-three years. The historian notes that Zhao Tuo’s rise was due to Ren Xiao, and the kingdom’s fall stemmed from internal conflicts and Lu Jia’s actions.

Wei Qing, a native of Pingyang County, was the illegitimate son of Zheng Ji and a concubine of the Pingyang Marquis household. His half-sister Wei Zifu gained favor with Emperor Wu of Han, leading Wei Qing to adopt the surname Wei. As a youth, he served as a servant and shepherd, enduring mistreatment from his half-brothers. A prisoner once prophesied his future nobility, but Wei Qing dismissed it. He later became a cavalryman for the Pingyang Marquis. When Wei Zifu entered the palace and became pregnant, Empress Chen, jealous, attempted to kill Wei Qing. His friend Gongsun Ao rescued him, and Emperor Wu subsequently appointed Wei Qing as a palace supervisor, elevating his status. Wei Zifu later became empress, and Wei Qing was promoted to Dazhong doctor.
In 129 BCE, Wei Qing led a cavalry attack on the Xiongnu, achieving modest success. Subsequent campaigns saw him capture the Henan region, driving out Xiongnu kings and establishing Shuofang Commandery. For these victories, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Changping. Further campaigns against the Xiongnu resulted in significant victories, including the capture of King Youxian's forces and vast numbers of livestock. Emperor Wu granted Wei Qing additional households and enfeoffed his sons as marquises, though Wei Qing humbly declined, crediting the emperor and his officers.
Wei Qing's nephew, Huo Qubing, emerged as a brilliant commander, earning the title of Champion Marquis for his daring raids. Huo Qubing's campaigns were marked by deep penetrations into Xiongnu territory, capturing kings and vast numbers of enemies. He became increasingly favored by the emperor, eventually matching Wei Qing in rank and power. Huo Qubing famously declined a mansion, stating, "The Xiongnu have not yet been eliminated, so I have no intention of considering private matters." However, he was known for his lack of concern for his soldiers' welfare, often discarding food while they starved. After Huo Qubing's death, Wei Qing's influence waned. Wei Qing died four years later, and his descendants lost their titles due to legal infractions. The text concludes with a list of Wei Qing's and Huo Qubing's subordinates, many of whom became generals or marquises. The historian Sima Qian notes that Wei Qing, despite his nobility, refrained from recruiting scholars, fearing the emperor's displeasure, a principle Huo Qubing also followed.

Sima Ranju, a descendant of Tian Wan, was recommended by Yan Ying to Qi Jinggong during a crisis when Jin and Yan attacked Qi. Despite his humble status, Ranju’s literary and military talents impressed the king, who appointed him general. Ranju requested a trusted minister, Zhuang Jia, to supervise the army. They agreed to meet at the camp gate at noon. Ranju arrived early and set up timing devices, but Zhuang Jia, delayed by farewell feasts, arrived at dusk. Ranju condemned his lateness, citing that a general must forsake family, friendships, and personal safety in war. He executed Zhuang Jia under military law, shocking the army.
When Qi Jinggong’s envoy arrived with a pardon, racing into camp, Ranju declared that generals in the field need not accept all royal orders. He executed the envoy’s servants and horses, parading them before the troops. Ranju then personally cared for soldiers, sharing provisions and tending to the sick. After three days, the army was revitalized. The Jin and Yan forces withdrew upon learning of this discipline, and Qi reclaimed lost territory. Returning in triumph, Ranju was appointed Grand Sima by Qi Jinggong, elevating the Tian family’s status. However, officials Bao, Gao, and Guo slandered him, leading to his dismissal and death from illness. The Tian family later retaliated, killing the Gao and Guo clans. Tian He, a descendant, became King Qi Wei, who imitated Ranju’s methods and incorporated his strategies into the “Sima’s Art of War.” Sima Qian notes that while Ranju’s achievements were for a small state, the “Sima’s Art of War” is profound, and he refrains from further commentary, presenting only this biography.

Lu Buwei, a wealthy merchant from Yangzhai, amassed a fortune through low-cost buying and high-price selling. During the reign of King Zhao of Qin, the crown prince died, and An Guojun was appointed as the new prince. An Guojun had many sons, including Zichu, a middle-ranking son sent as a hostage to Zhao. Zichu, neglected and impoverished, caught Lu Buwei's attention. Lu Buwei saw him as a rare commodity to be hoarded and offered to help him gain power. Lu Buwei traveled to Qin to lobby An Guojun and his favored concubine, Mrs. Huayang, who had no son. He persuaded Mrs. Huayang to adopt Zichu as her heir, ensuring her future influence. An Guojun agreed, and Zichu became the designated heir. Lu Buwei gave Zichu funds and married him to a beautiful dancer, Zhao Ji, who bore a son, Ying Zheng.
During a siege of Handan, Zichu escaped to Qin with Lu Buwei's help. After King Zhao's death, An Guojun became king, and Zichu became prince. An Guojun died shortly after, and Zichu ascended as King Zhuang Xiang, appointing Lu Buwei as prime minister. King Zhuang Xiang died three years later, and Ying Zheng became king, with Lu Buwei as regent.
Lu Buwei, competing with other lords, hosted 3,000 scholars and compiled the *Lüshi Chunqiu*, a comprehensive text. He later introduced Lao Ai, a man with a large penis, to the Queen Mother, who had an affair with him. Lao Ai gained power and fathered two sons with her. When discovered, Lao Ai rebelled but was executed. Lu Buwei was implicated, dismissed, and exiled. Fearing further persecution, he committed suicide by drinking poison.

Mengchangjun, whose surname was Tian and given name Wen, was the son of Jingguo Jun Tian Ying. Tian Ying, the youngest son of King Qi Wei, served as a general and later as prime minister of Qi, leading campaigns against Wei and forming alliances with Han and Wei. He had over forty sons, but Tian Wen was born on May 5th, a date considered inauspicious. Tian Ying ordered the child abandoned, but his mother secretly raised him. When Tian Wen grew up, he confronted his father, arguing that fate was determined by heaven, not by the doorframe, and criticized Tian Ying for accumulating wealth while neglecting the state's welfare. Impressed, Tian Ying made Tian Wen his heir.
After Tian Ying's death, Tian Wen inherited the title of Lord Mengchang in Xue Yi. He generously hosted thousands of guests, treating them equally regardless of status. He recorded their conversations and sent gifts to their relatives. Once, a guest suspected unequal treatment, but Lord Mengchang compared his own meal to prove fairness, leading the guest to commit suicide in shame. Lord Mengchang accepted all guests without discrimination, earning their loyalty.
King Zhao of Qin, hearing of Lord Mengchang's virtue, invited him to Qin and appointed him prime minister. However, officials warned that Lord Mengchang, being a Qi noble, would prioritize Qi's interests, so King Zhao imprisoned him. Lord Mengchang's concubine demanded his white fox fur as a bribe for her intercession. A guest skilled in thievery disguised himself as a dog, stole the fur from the palace, and gave it to the concubine, who secured Lord Mengchang's release. As he fled, another guest imitated a rooster's crow to open the Hangu Pass gates before pursuers arrived. Though initially ashamed of these lowly guests, Lord Mengchang's reliance on them earned admiration for his inclusive recruitment.
Later, Lord Mengchang became Qi's prime minister and planned to attack Qin with Han and Wei. Su Dai advised him to avoid strengthening Han and Wei, instead using the Western Zhou to negotiate with Qin for Chu's eastern territory and the release of King Huai of Chu. Lord Mengchang agreed, averting war. When dismissed as prime minister due to slander, he retired to Xue Yi. After Qin's general Lu Li became Qi's prime minister, Lord Mengchang, following Su Dai's advice, marched north to secure alliances, causing Lu Li to flee. When King Qi Min grew proud and sought to eliminate him, Lord Mengchang fled to Wei, became prime minister, and allied with Qin and Zhao to attack Qi, leading to King Min's death. King Xiang of Qi later reconciled with Lord Mengchang, who remained neutral among the states. After his death, his sons fought over the title, and Qi and Wei destroyed Xue Yi, ending his lineage.
Feng Chen, a poor scholar, joined Lord Mengchang's household. Initially placed in low-class quarters, he sang about lacking fish, a carriage, and means to support his family, prompting Lord Mengchang to upgrade his status. When Lord Mengchang needed to collect debts in Xue Yi, Feng Chen was sent. Instead of collecting, he burned the deeds of the poor, arguing that this would earn the people's trust and enhance Lord Mengchang's reputation. Though initially angry, Lord Mengchang later thanked him. When Lord Mengchang was dismissed as prime minister, his guests abandoned him. When Wu'anhou Tianfu became prime minister, high-ranking officials knelt to him, but Ji An only bowed. The emperor, recruiting literary scholars, was rebuked by Ji An for having many desires while feigning benevolence. The emperor grew angry, and ministers feared for Ji An. Later, the emperor remarked on Ji An's stupidity, but Ji An defended his integrity, stating he would not harm court affairs. Ill for three months, Ji An's condition persisted. Zhuang Zhu, requesting leave on his behalf, told the emperor that Ji An could assist a young monarch steadfastly, unswayed by inducements or threats. The emperor agreed, comparing Ji An to ancient loyal ministers.
General Wei Qing entered the palace with the emperor seated by his bed, while Prime Minister Gongsun Hong sometimes saw the emperor without a hat. For Ji An, the emperor always wore a hat, once hiding in a tent when unprepared. Ji An was highly respected. When Zhang Tang became a court official, Ji An accused him of failing to uphold the late emperor's achievements and changing rules set by Emperor Gaozu, warning of lost descendants. They often argued, with Ji An scolding Zhang Tang for causing fear. The Han Dynasty was then conquering the Xiongnu, and Ji An advised peace, but the emperor favored Confucianism and Gongsun Hong. Ji An criticized Gongsun Hong and Zhang Tang as treacherous, leading to their deep hatred. Gongsun Hong suggested Ji An as Right Internal History to manage dignitaries, a role Ji An handled well for years. General Wei Qing's status rose, but Ji An treated him as an equal. When advised to kneel, Ji An replied that bowing did not diminish respect. Wei Qing valued Ji An's virtue, seeking his advice. Liu An, the king of Huainan, feared Ji An's integrity, noting it was hard to tempt him. As Ji An enjoyed Jiuqing treatment, Gongsun Hong and Zhang Tang rose to equal ranks, then surpassed him. Ji An complained to the emperor about later officials being piled on top, but the emperor dismissed his stupidity. When King Hunxie of the Xiongnu surrendered, the court borrowed horses from the people, causing unrest. Ji An defended the magistrate of Chang'an, suggesting gradual preparations. Later, over 500 merchants were sentenced to death for trading with the Huns. Ji An argued against harsh laws, but the emperor disagreed. Months later, Ji An was convicted of a minor law, dismissed, and retired.
Years later, the emperor appointed Ji An as prefect of Huaiyang County due to private coin minting. Ji An declined but was forced to accept. He managed the county well, and after Zhang Tang's ruin, the emperor ordered Ji An to enjoy princes' salary while governing Huaiyang. Ji An died seven years later. His brother Ji Ren and son Ji Yan were promoted, and his aunt's son Sima An reached Jiuqing four times. Duan Hong from Puyang also rose to Jiuqing, but officials respected Ji An more.
Zheng Zhuang, courtesy name Zhuang, was born in Chen County. His ancestor Zheng Jun served under Xiang Ji and refused to address him by his first name, as ordered by Emperor Gaozu, leading to his dismissal. Zheng Zhuang was chivalrous, rescuing Zhang Yu, and gained fame in Liang and Chu. During Emperor Xiao Jing's reign, he served as Prince Sheren, often visiting friends and hosting guests. He loved Taoism, admired elders, and was humble. Under Emperor Wu, he rose to Right Internal History of Jiuqing but was demoted for improper opinions. As Right Internal History, he treated visitors equally, was upright, and had no private property, using his salary to support friends. He recommended scholars, praising them as better than himself, and was praised by elders east of Miao Mountain. Sent to inspect the Yellow River breach, he asked for five days to prepare, but the emperor noted his reputation for traveling without food. In later years, due to debts from recommended guests, he was demoted to civilian, then served as governor of Runan County until death. Zheng Zhuang and Ji An were both honest, dismissed, and poor, with no property after death. Six or seven of Zheng Zhuang's descendants reached two thousand shi. Tai Shigong noted that Ji An and Zheng Zhuang's virtue attracted many guests when powerful, but few when powerless. Zhai Gong of Xiajun County wrote on his gate: "One death and one life show friendship; one poor and one rich show acquaintance; one noble and one humble show friendship." Ji An and Zheng Zhuang suffered this misfortune, which was sad.

Confucius stated that the Six Classics serve the same purpose in governing a country: "Li" regulates conduct, "Music" promotes harmony, "Book" records past deeds, "Poetry" expresses emotions, "Yi" explores cosmic changes, and "Spring and Autumn" discerns subtle meanings and right from wrong. Tai Shigong remarked on the vastness of truth, noting that concise words can resolve many troubles. Chunyu Kun, a short, witty son-in-law of Qi, often served as an envoy without disgrace. During King Wei of Qi's reign, the king neglected state affairs, indulging in feasting and drinking, leading to invasions and national peril. No minister dared to advise. Chunyu Kun used an allegory of a great bird that neither flew nor cried for three years. King Wei understood, summoned all county chiefs, rewarded one, executed another, and repelled invaders, restoring Qi's prestige for 36 years. Later, when Chu invaded, Chunyu Kun was sent to Zhao for reinforcements with modest gifts. He laughed at a farmer praying for abundant harvests with meager offerings, prompting King Wei to increase the gifts. Zhao then sent 100,000 elite troops, causing Chu to withdraw. King Wei asked Chunyu Kun about his drinking capacity. Chunyu Kun explained that his drunkenness varied by context: fear made him drunk after one measure, while joy allowed him to drink eight measures. He warned against excess, as it leads to decline. King Wei ceased nightly drinking and appointed Chunyu Kun as a guest official.
Over a century later, You Meng, a tall Chu performer, used humor to advise King Zhuang. When the king wanted to bury his beloved horse with grand rites, You Meng suggested an even grander burial to expose the king's folly. King Zhuang relented and had the horse cooked. Later, You Meng impersonated the deceased prime minister Sun Shuao to advise King Zhuang. He highlighted Sun Shuao's poverty despite his integrity, leading the king to grant Sun's son land and households for ancestral worship.
Two centuries later, You Zhan, a short Qin performer, used wit to aid others. During a rainstorm, he joked about guards being wet while he was dry, leading Qin Shihuang to halve their duty. He also dissuaded the emperor from expanding hunting grounds and Qin Ershi from painting city walls, using humor to highlight impracticality.
Tai Shigong praised these three for their clever advice. Mr. Chu Shaosun added six more tales, including that of Guo Sheren, who helped a wet nurse avoid exile by prompting her to show reluctance, moving Emperor Wu to pity. Dongfang Shuo, a learned scholar, used humor to gain favor with Emperor Wu, often receiving rewards but spending them on marriages. He defended his behavior as "court reclusion" and advised against slander on his deathbed. Mr. Dong Guo advised General Wei Qing to gift gold to Empress Wang's parents, earning himself an official post. Other tales include a clever envoy who lost a swan but gained rewards, a prefect coached by a drunkard to credit the emperor for peace, and Ximen Bao, who stopped the practice of sacrificing girls to the River God by throwing the corrupt priests into the river, then dug irrigation canals that benefited the people for generations.

Bai Qi, a skilled military commander from Yidi, served King Zhao of Qin. His early campaigns included victories against Han, Wei, and Zhao, capturing cities and killing tens of thousands of enemies. He was promoted through ranks, eventually becoming Lord Wu'an after conquering Chu's capital Ying and burning its royal tombs. His most notable battle was against Zhao at Changping in the 47th year of King Zhao's reign. After initial setbacks, Zhao replaced General Lian Po with Zhao Kuo. Bai Qi used deception, cutting off Zhao's supply lines and surrounding their army. After 46 days without food, Zhao Kuo was killed, and 400,000 Zhao soldiers surrendered. Bai Qi, fearing rebellion, ordered them buried alive, shocking Zhao. Following this, Qin planned to besiege Handan, but Su Dai, sent by Han and Zhao, persuaded Prime Minister Yinghou to halt, arguing that Bai Qi's growing fame threatened Yinghou's position. King Zhao agreed to a truce, but Bai Qi's resentment toward Yinghou grew. When Qin later attacked Handan under Wang Ling, Bai Qi refused to lead, citing the army's exhaustion and the risk of allied reinforcements. Despite King Zhao's orders, Bai Qi feigned illness. After Qin's defeat, Bai Qi's remarks angered the king, who demoted him and ordered his exile. Accused of discontent, Bai Qi was forced to commit suicide in the 50th year of King Zhao's reign.
Wang Jian, from Pinyang, served Qin Shihuang. He conquered Zhao, Yan, and other states, often requesting 600,000 troops for campaigns. After Li Xin's failed attack on Chu with 200,000 men, Wang Jian was recalled. He led 600,000 troops, avoided direct engagement, and waited for Chu's army to weaken before striking, defeating them and capturing King Chu. Wang Jian's son Wang Ben and Li Xin later conquered Yan and Qi, unifying China. Wang Jian's grandson Wang Li, a third-generation general, was captured by Xiang Yu during Chen Sheng's rebellion, fulfilling a saying that general families often fail by the third generation due to accumulated killings.
Sima Qian noted Bai Qi's strategic brilliance but inability to avoid Yinghou's schemes, and Wang Jian's military success but failure to promote moral governance, leading to his grandson's capture.

Fan Ju, a man of eloquence, initially sought to serve the King of Wei but was too poor to fund his journey. He first served under Xu Jia, a senior official in Wei. When Xu Jia was sent as an envoy to Qi, Fan Ju accompanied him. King Qi Xiang, impressed by Fan Ju's eloquence, sent him gifts of gold, beef, and wine, which Fan Ju refused. Xu Jia suspected Fan Ju had betrayed Wei secrets to Qi and reported this to the Wei prime minister, Wei Qi. Wei Qi had Fan Ju beaten severely, breaking his ribs and teeth, then wrapped him in a mat and threw him in a toilet, where drunken guests urinated on him. Fan Ju convinced a guard to let him escape, and later hid with the help of Zheng Anping, changing his name to Zhang Lu.
When King Zhao of Qin sent envoy Wang Ji to Wei, Zheng Anping arranged a secret meeting between Fan Ju and Wang Ji. Recognizing Fan Ju's talent, Wang Ji took him to Qin. On the way, they encountered Marquis Rang, the powerful Qin prime minister, but Fan Ju hid to avoid detection. Once in Qin, Wang Ji recommended Fan Ju to King Zhao, but the king was skeptical and housed Fan Ju poorly for over a year. During this time, Qin had expanded its territory significantly, but the king distrusted lobbyists. Marquis Rang and other relatives of the queen mother held immense power, with private wealth exceeding the state's. Fan Ju wrote to King Zhao, arguing that a wise ruler rewards merit and talent, and that he was willing to die if his advice proved useless. Impressed, King Zhao summoned Fan Ju. At the palace, Fan Ju deliberately provoked the king by claiming Qin only had a queen mother and Marquis Rang, not a king. King Zhao apologized for the delay and sought Fan Ju's counsel. After three rounds of questioning, Fan Ju finally spoke, citing historical examples to emphasize the importance of trust and the dangers of powerful relatives. He outlined a strategy of befriending distant states and attacking nearby ones, starting with Han and Wei, to consolidate Qin's power. The historian comments that Fan Ju and Cai泽 succeeded in Qin due to the state's strength and their own perseverance through hardship, noting that many talented individuals fail without such opportunities.
King Zhao appointed Fan Ju as a guest minister and followed his advice, capturing cities from Wei and Han. Over time, Fan Ju gained the king's trust and exposed the overreach of the queen mother and Marquis Rang, leading to their expulsion. Fan Ju became prime minister, and the king granted him the title of Marquis Ying. When Xu Jia later visited Qin as an envoy, Fan Ju humiliated him for past wrongs but spared his life due to a gift of a robe. Fan Ju also recommended Zheng Anping as a general and repaid all who had helped him.
However, Fan Ju's later years were troubled. Zheng Anping surrendered to Zhao, and Wang Ji was executed for colluding with other states. King Zhao expressed concern about Qin's lack of capable generals, unsettling Fan Ju. Cai Ze, a strategist from Yan, then arrived and warned Fan Ju of the dangers of holding power too long, citing historical figures like Shang Yang and Wu Qi who died after their achievements. Fan Ju heeded the advice and recommended Cai Ze to King Zhao, eventually resigning as prime minister. Cai Ze served briefly but also resigned due to slander, living on in Qin for many years.

When Wang Mang usurped the Han throne, loyal scholars refused to serve him, preferring poverty and seclusion. Although Guangwu revived the Han, the issue of serving in office remained critical. Biographies of several individuals from the Han dynasty. Liu Ping, originally named Kuang, was from Pengcheng. During Wang Mang's time, he was a county official. During the Gengshi period, when thieves arrived, he fled with his mother, abandoning his own son to save his orphaned niece. He later encountered a hungry thief who wanted to eat him, but Liu Ping begged to feed his mother first and promised to return. The thief, moved by his sincerity, let him go. Liu Ping kept his promise and returned, but the thief spared him. In the early Jianwu years, he risked his life to protect the wounded governor Sun Meng, suffering seven stab wounds and even offering his own blood to the thirsty Sun Meng. Liu Ping was later promoted to Xiaolian and became Prime Minister of Jiyin County. He was later recommended by Zhongliyi and served as Yilang and Zongzheng, recommending famous scholars. He died at home after requesting retirement due to old age and illness.
Zhao Xiao, named Changnian, was from Peiguo. His father served under Wang Mang. Zhao Xiao was known for his humility, traveling in plain clothes. During a famine, his brother Zhao Li was captured by hungry thieves. Zhao Xiao bound himself and went to the thieves, offering his own fatter body in exchange. The thieves released them. He was later recruited and served as an admonishing official and Changle Guardsman. His brother Zhao Li also became an official. The emperor favored them, but Zhao Li died a few years later. Zhao Xiao died at home after returning from leave. Chunyu Gong, named Meng Sun, was from Beihai. He was a quiet man who studied Laozi. When someone stole his fruit, he helped them harvest it. When he saw a thief stealing seedlings, he hid to avoid shaming him. During a famine, he offered to replace his brother Chunyu Chong who was about to be cooked by bandits, and both were spared. He raised his brother's children, disciplining them by beating himself. He continued to farm despite chaos. He refused multiple calls to serve, living in seclusion for decades. Emperor Suzong eventually summoned him, made him a counselor, and later promoted him. He died in office, and the emperor ordered a stone carving to commend him.
Jiang Ge, named Cweng, was from Linzi. He fled with his mother on his back during chaos, picking wild fruits to survive. When thieves tried to kidnap him, he cried and begged, saying his mother depended on him, and the thieves spared him. He worked to support his mother in poverty. After returning home, he pulled his mother in a cart himself, earning the nickname "Jiang Da Duozi." He refused official invitations due to his mother's age. After her death, he slept by her tomb. He was later promoted to Xiaolian and served as Taipu of Chu, but abandoned the post. He later served as Sikong Changshi and General of the Five Features. The emperor treated him with great respect. He refused gifts from nobles. He requested retirement and was made an admonishing doctor. The emperor later issued an edict praising his filial piety and ordered the county to give him gifts.
Liu Ban was the great-great-grandson of Emperor Xuan. His father Liu Yu raised his younger brother Liu Ping after their mother died, and died of grief after Liu Ping's death. Liu Ban lived with his mother during Wang Mang's failure. He studied diligently despite his family's concerns. In the eighth year of Jianwu, he moved to Luoyang to study. He was later enfeoffed as a marquis. The emperor commended him for his good conduct. He served as Jinwu and captain of the cavalry school. He advised against establishing the Changpingcang, arguing it would harm the people. He also argued against a ban on farmers engaging in fishing and hunting, and against officials inflating land cultivation figures. He died at age sixty.
Zhou Pan, named Jianbo, was from Runan. He studied classics and was known for his good conduct. He left his official post to return home when he missed his mother. After his mother died, he lived next to her grave and taught thousands of disciples. He refused multiple government calls, saying he had no need for external things after his mother's death. At age seventy-three, he predicted his death, gave his sons instructions for a simple burial with a copy of the "Yao Canon," and died without illness. Zhao Zi, named Wenchu, was from Dongjun. He was known for his filial piety. When robbers came to his house, he asked them to leave some food for his sick mother. The robbers, ashamed, left. He was later summoned to be an official and became Prime Minister of the East China Sea. He was known for his frugality. Before his death, he instructed his son to use a simple, thin coffin to allow his body to decay quickly and return to the earth. He wrote a long suicide note criticizing lavish burials and advocating for simplicity, citing ancient examples. His son followed his instructions.

Biographies of several virtuous men from the Later Han period, emphasizing their moral integrity, reclusiveness, and resistance to officialdom. **Jiang Gong**, from Pengcheng, was renowned for filial piety and brotherly love, sleeping with his brothers even after marriage. He taught the Five Classics to over 3,000 students but refused all official positions. When encountering bandits, he and his brother vied to die for each other, moving the thieves to repentance. Later, he feigned illness to avoid being painted for the emperor and fled to the coast to escape eunuch-dominated politics, living in obscurity until his death at seventy-seven.
**Zhou Xie**, from Runan, was born with a disfigured face that his mother wanted to abandon, but his father kept him, foreseeing his future prosperity. He was a precocious child, mastering classics like the *Book of Songs* and *Analects* by age ten, and later specializing in the *Book of Rites* and *Book of Changes*. He lived self-sufficiently, farming and fishing, and refused to eat what he did not produce. Despite being recommended for office multiple times, he feigned illness to avoid service. Eventually, he accepted a summons but soon returned home, citing the difficulty of moving with the times. He died in his seventies.
**Huang Xian**, also from Runan, was born into a poor family, his father being a cattle doctor. At fourteen, he impressed the scholar Xun Shu, who declared him a teacher. His profound character was noted by contemporaries: Dai Liang felt humbled in his presence, and Chen Fan admitted that seeing Huang Xian curbed his own stinginess. Guo Linzong compared him to vast, immeasurable waters. Huang Xian was recommended for office but never took up a post, dying at forty-eight. **Xu Zhen**, from Yuzhang, was a poor farmer who refused to eat unearned food. He briefly served as a merit officer under Prefect Chen Fan, who set up a special couch for him. He repeatedly declined official summons, including from Emperor Huan. After the death of Taiwei Huang Qiong, Xu Zhen traveled to mourn anonymously. He was known for his subtle acts of respect, such as leaving a bundle of grass at Guo Linzong's mother's funeral. He died at seventy-two.
**Shen Tu Pan**, from Chenliu, mourned his father excessively, abstaining from meat and wine for over a decade. At fifteen, he successfully pleaded for a woman avenging her father. He lived in poverty, working as a painter, and was praised by Cai Yong. He refused official posts, including from Taiwei Huang Qiong, and predicted the disaster of the Partisan Prohibitions, which he escaped by living in seclusion. He died at seventy-four, maintaining his principles through turbulent times.

Zhang Heng, styled Pingzi, was a native of Xi'e County, Nanyang. His grandfather, Zhang Kan, served as the prefect of Shu County. Zhang Heng excelled in writing from a young age, studied in Sanfu and the Imperial Academy, and mastered the Five Classics and Six Arts. Despite his exceptional talent, he remained humble and indifferent, avoiding interactions with common people. During the Yongyuan period of Emperor He, he was recommended as a Xiaolian but declined multiple government recruitments. Observing the extravagance of the time, he spent ten years composing "Ode to Two Capitals" as a satire, inspired by Ban Gu's work. General Deng Zhi admired his talent but Zhang Heng ignored his summons. Skilled in mechanics, astronomy, yin-yang, and calendar calculation, Zhang Heng admired Yang Xiong's "Tai Xuan Jing." Emperor An appointed him as a doctor and later as Taishi Ling, where he studied yin-yang, built an armillary sphere, and wrote "Lingxian" and "Suanwang Lun." In the first year of Yangjia, he created a seismoscope made of fine copper, eight feet in diameter, with eight dragons holding copper balls and toads beneath them. When an earthquake occurred, a dragon would release a ball into a toad's mouth, indicating the direction. This device proved accurate, even detecting a distant earthquake in Longxi that others initially doubted.
As political affairs declined, Zhang Heng advised the emperor against sharing power with subordinates, warning that disasters stemmed from moral failings. He criticized prophecies as false, noting they emerged only after the Cheng and Ai periods and contradicted classical texts. He urged their suppression to prevent confusion.
Later, as Prime Minister of Hejian, Zhang Heng curbed the king's arrogance and lawlessness, earning a reputation for integrity. After three years, he requested retirement and died at sixty-two. He authored thirty-two works, including poems and essays. He also sought to correct historical records, arguing that Wang Mang's biography should focus on usurpation and that Gengshi's title should precede Guangwu's, but his proposals were not accepted. The historian praised his profound wisdom and mechanical ingenuity, noting that his virtue was not diminished by his skills.

Xu Man, from Pingyu, Runan, inherited his grandfather Xu Jun's divination skills. During Emperor Huan's reign, Prefect Feng Zui saw two red snakes escape when opening his ribbon. Xu Man divined that in three years, Zui would become a border general named Dongming, traveling three thousand miles northeast, and in five years, a general marching south. In the first year of Yanxi, Feng Zui became governor of Liaodong, attacking Xianbei, and in the fifth year, general of chariots and cavalry, attacking Wuling barbarians, as divined. Zhao Yan, from Langyi, had skills. In the third year of Yanxi, thieves killed the captain and captured Langfu County. The court sent Nanyang Zongzi to attack. Zhao Yan explained the method of "Gu Xu", advising to mobilize Wuyang soldiers to attack Guxu. Zongzi reported, and an edict sent Wuyang soldiers. Zhao Yan pushed Dunjia, teaching them to advance at the right time, defeating the traitors in one battle and burning their camps, pacifying Xuzhou and Yanzhou. Fan Zhi Zhang, from Nanzheng, Hanzhong, was learned and versatile, living in seclusion. He traveled to Longxi and was sent by Qiang general Duan Zhen to conquer the Western Qiang. Surrounded by Qiang, Fan advised that there were no Qiang in the southeast corner, so they could escape and later return to win. Duan obeyed and defeated the traitor. Fan was praised as having the knowledge of Zi Shen, Jiao Yanshou, and Dong Zhongshu, and a special edict was issued, but Fan died of illness.
Guo Yu, from Luo, Guanghan, studied under Cheng Gao, learning the skills of diagnosing the six subtleties and calculating yin and yang. During Emperor He's reign, he became imperial physician. Once, the emperor asked him to diagnose a favored minister and a woman hiding in a tent. Guo Yu said there was yang on the left and yin on the right, suspecting a strange person. The emperor praised him. Guo Yu was kind-hearted, treating poor servants diligently but sometimes ineffective with nobles. The emperor asked a noble to wear ragged clothes, and the disease was cured with one injection. Guo Yu explained that nobles had four difficulties: self-decision, lack of care, weak joints, and inactivity, making treatment difficult. He died while serving as imperial physician.
Hua Tuo, courtesy name Yuanhua, from Pei State, was proficient in scriptures and knew how to cultivate his nature. He was recommended as Xiaolian but did not take the post. He was skilled in prescriptions and acupuncture, using Mafei San for surgery. He cured a man with a throat disease by having him drink sour water chestnuts, causing him to vomit a snake. He treated a county governor by making him angry, causing him to vomit black blood and recover. He performed a caesarean section on a patient, who died ten years later. He cured Chen Deng of worms, but the disease relapsed after three years when Hua Tuo died. Cao Cao summoned Hua Tuo for his head wind, and acupuncture relieved it. Hua Tuo asked for leave, claiming his wife was sick, but Cao Cao discovered the lie and imprisoned him. Despite Xun Yu's plea, Cao Cao killed Hua Tuo. Before death, Hua Tuo gave a medical book to the jailer, who refused, so he burned it. Wu Pu and Fan A studied under Hua Tuo. Wu Pu practiced the Wu Qin Xi, living over ninety with good health. Fan A knew acupuncture, using deep needles effectively. Hua Tuo gave him Lacquer Leaf Qingnian Powder, and Fan A lived over a hundred years.
Xu Deng, from Fujian, was originally a woman who became a husband, good at witchcraft. Zhao Bing, from Dongyang, could serve Yue Fang. During a military turmoil and epidemic, they met on the Wushang River and shared their magic to cure diseases. Xu Deng banned the stream, stopping water flow; Zhao Bing banned a withered tree, making it sprout. They practiced together, with Zhao Bing treating Xu Deng as teacher. They advocated frugality, using east flowing water for worship and mulberry bark for dried meat. Xu Deng died, and Zhao Bing went eastward to Zhang'an. He used a plane tree trunk to support a pot to cook, surprising the owner but not damaging the house. He crossed a river with an umbrella, passing through turbulent currents. The magistrate of Zhang'an arrested and killed him for sorcery. The people built a temple for him in Yongkang, where no mosquitoes enter.
Fei Changfang, from Runan, served as a city official. An old man selling medicine jumped into a pot, and Changfang saw this. The old man took him into the pot, where there was a jade hall with fine wine. The old man, a god punished for a mistake, asked Changfang to go with him. Changfang feared his family would worry, so the old man cut a bamboo stick, hung it behind the house, and the family thought Changfang had hanged himself. Changfang followed the old man into the mountains, facing tigers and snakes without fear. The old man asked him to eat feces, but Changfang felt disgusted. The old man said he was almost enlightened but failed this test. He gave Changfang a bamboo stick to ride home and a talisman to dominate ghosts and gods. Changfang returned, finding more than ten years had passed. He threw the bamboo stick into a pond, and it turned into a dragon. He cured diseases, drove away ghosts, and interrogated criminals. He once caught a ghost that transformed into an old turtle. He locked up Lord Donghai for three years, causing a drought, then released him to make rain. He caught a fox stealing the land father-in-law's horse. Later, his talisman was lost, and he was killed by ghosts.
Ji Zi Xun, from unknown origin, lived in Wanju, Jiyin during the Jian'an period. He had magical spells. He once hugged a neighbor's baby, let it fall to the ground and die, then buried it. More than a month later, he returned with the baby alive. The parents were panicked, but the baby knew them, and they accepted it. They dug up the grave and found only clothes. Zi Xun's name spread, and scholar-bureaucrats admired him. He drove a donkey cart to Xuxia. Passing through Xingyang, his donkey died and maggots crawled out. He beat it with a stick, and the donkey got up and walked. Thousands of people followed to watch. In the capital, hundreds of people waited for him, including ministers. He later escaped, and no one knew where he went. A centenarian said he saw Zi Xun selling medicine in Kuaiji City as a child, with the same face. Later, someone saw him in Dongba City, Chang'an, rubbing bronze figures with an old man, saying they had been made for nearly five hundred years. The person called him, but he walked slowly, and the horse could not catch up. Liu Gen, from Yingchuan, lived in seclusion in Songshan Mountain. Some good people came to learn Taoism from him. The prefect Shi Qi thought he was a monster, arrested him, and demanded he show a god or be executed. Liu Gen said he could make people see ghosts. He looked back and let out a roar, and Shi Qi's dead father and ancestors walked forward, kowtowing to Liu Gen and scolding Shi Qi. Shi Qi kowtowed and begged for mercy, but Liu Gen refused and left, unknown to where.
Zuo Ci, courtesy name Yuanfang, from Lujiang, received Shinto at a young age. He was a guest at Cao Cao's place. Cao Cao said they lacked seabass from Wu Songjiang. Zuo Ci fished into a copper plate with water and caught a bass. He caught more fish, all over three feet long. Cao Cao said they lacked ginger from Sichuan. Zuo Ci obtained it and also brought a reply from Cao Cao's envoy. Later, Cao Cao traveled to the suburbs with over a hundred officials. Zuo Ci poured wine for everyone with a liter of wine and a pound of dried meat, and all were drunk and full. Cao Cao investigated and found the taverns missing wine and meat. He imprisoned Zuo Ci, but Zuo Ci fled into the wall. Someone found him in the market, but everyone in the city had the same image. Later, someone encountered him on Yangcheng Mountain and chased him into a flock of sheep. Cao Cao sent someone to say he would not kill him, and an old ram stood up and spoke. The pursuers rushed into the flock, but hundreds of sheep turned into old rams, all speaking, and they could not catch him.

Zhu Fu, courtesy name Shu Yuan, was from Xiao, Pei State. He initially served under Guangwu, followed him to break Handan, and was later appointed General Youzhou Mu to guard Jicheng and settle the northern border. In the second year of Jianwu, he was made Marquis of Wuyang. Zhu Fu sought to revive his reputation by recruiting famous scholars and former officials of Wang Mang, which angered Peng Chong, the prefect of Yuyang, who refused to comply. Zhu Fu slandered Peng Chong, leading to resentment. Zhu Fu reported Peng Chong for various offenses, and Peng Chong, enraged, raised troops to attack Zhu Fu. Zhu Fu reproached Peng Chong in a letter, criticizing his rebellion and comparing his merits to a Liaodong pig. Peng Chong attacked more fiercely, and despite Zhu Fu’s pleas for imperial aid, the court only sent Deng Long to assist. Zhu Fu fled after his city fell, and his wife was killed. The emperor replaced him as Jinwu and later as Marquis of Chengdu. After Peng Chong and Zhang Feng failed, Zhu Fu wrote a memorial criticizing the emperor’s harsh governance, advocating for slower, more careful administration. The emperor agreed, reducing mobilizations. Zhu Fu later served as a servant and proposed expanding the selection of doctors for the Imperial Academy, which the emperor approved. In the Yongping period, Zhu Fu was sentenced to death on false accusations, but Fan Wei interceded, and the emperor repented. The historian noted that Zhu Fu’s criticism of haste led to his death.
Feng Li, courtesy name Xiaosun, was from Huyang, Nanyang. During Wang Mang’s reign, he gathered guests and built a camp. He once saved Shentu Ji from Yu Duwei’s cousin, earning respect. Guangwu summoned him in the third year of Jianwu, making him magistrate of Yu County, where he governed with prestige. Later, as magistrate of Jiaxian, he fought bandits led by Yan Bao, who surrendered after Guangwu’s arrival. Feng Li pardoned them, and they served as informants, pacifying the county. He later served as prefect of Wei County and was appointed imperial servant of Zhao. In the Zhongyuan period, he became Sikong and Marquis of Guannei. After Guangwu’s death, he built the original mausoleum. In Yongping, he was dismissed for scrutinizing Deng Rong but later resumed duties. He served as King Wu of Yin Song, giving loyal advice. He retired due to old age in Jianchu and died at eighty-six.
Yu Yan, courtesy name Zi Da, was from Chenliu. Born with an auspicious sign, he was strong and tall. As a youth, he arrested a noble’s guests, earning resentment. During Wang Mang’s chaos, he defended his relatives. He adopted his cousin’s abandoned infant. As magistrate of Xiyang County, he let prisoners go home for the new year; they returned as promised. He resigned after advising Prefect Fu Zong against extravagance; Fu Zong was later executed. Guangwu, impressed, appointed Yu Yan as governor. He served as Luoyang magistrate, punishing the Yin family’s guest Ma Cheng despite pleas. He later became Nanyang governor. In Yongping, he recognized Deng Yan’s lack of manners, leading to Deng Yan’s shame. Yu Yan served as Taiwei and Situ, but when Liu Ying of Chu rebelled, Yu Yan failed to report contacts, leading to his suicide. His family was left poor.
Zheng Hong, from Kuaiji, was a misfit as a youth but was recognized by Prefect Wu Lun. He studied under Jiao Kuang, who was implicated in Liu Ying’s rebellion. When Jiao Kuang died, Zheng Hong shaved his head and pleaded for his family, gaining fame. As magistrate of Zuxian, he governed benevolently. He became Shangshu Ling and proposed that Shangshu Lang supplement Thousand Stone Orders, which the emperor accepted. As chief agricultural officer, he opened mountain roads in Lingling and Guiyang, saving three trillion in assets. He reduced contributions and corvee fees during drought. As Taiwei, he deferred to the Fifth Lun, and the emperor set up a screen between them. He reported Zhang Lin and Yang Guang for corruption, but Dou Xian accused him of leaking secrets. Zheng Hong resigned and died, leaving instructions for a simple burial. Zhou Zhang, from Nanyang, was a meritorious official. He advised the prefect against privately visiting Dou Xian, cutting the horse’s leather to stop him. When Dou Xian was executed, the prefect was spared. Zhou Zhang became Guang Luxun and later Sikong. He criticized Zheng Zhong and Cai Lun’s power. After Emperor He’s death, Empress Dowager Deng made Liu Sheng king of Pingyuan and later Emperor An. Zhou Zhang plotted to kill Deng Zhi, Zheng Zhong, and Cai Lun, depose the queen, and make Liu Sheng emperor. The plot was discovered, and Zhou Zhang committed suicide, leaving no wealth. The historian warned against such usurpation, citing Mencius.

Huan Rong, courtesy name Chunqing, was a native of Longkang, Pei County. He studied the "Ouyang Shangshu" under Zhu Pu in Chang'an, supporting himself through servant labor. He did not return home for fifteen years, only returning after Wang Mang's usurpation. After Zhu Pu's death, Huan Rong built his grave and stayed to teach, amassing hundreds of disciples. During the chaos following Wang Mang's fall, he fled into the valleys with his students, continuing to lecture despite hunger. Later, he taught in the Jianghuai region. In the 19th year of Jianwu, over sixty, Huan Rong was appointed Grand Situ. When Xianzong became crown prince, Huan Rong's student He Tang was chosen to teach him the "Book of Documents." The emperor summoned Huan Rong, was impressed by his explanation of "Shang Shu," and appointed him Yilang, allowing him to teach the prince. Huan Rong declined a promotion to Dr. Ouyang, recommending his disciples Peng Hong and Gao Hong instead. He was later made a doctor. The emperor praised his gentle, erudite manner and rewarded him. Huan Rong served as the prince's young tutor, and after the prince's studies were complete, he requested retirement but was persuaded to stay. He was later appointed Taichang. When Xianzong ascended the throne, Huan Rong was honored as a master of etiquette. He repeatedly requested retirement due to old age, receiving additional rewards each time. The emperor visited him, showing great respect. Huan Rong died after a long illness, and the emperor personally attended his funeral and granted him a tomb.
Ding Hong, courtesy name Xiaogong, was a native of Dingling, Yingchuan. His father, Ding Lin, surrendered Yingyang to Shizu and was rewarded, later becoming Governor of Henan. Ding Lin chose to be enfeoffed in his hometown, becoming Marquis of Xin'an Township. Ding Hong studied "Ouyang Shangshu" under Huan Rong at thirteen, mastering it in three years. After his father's death, he attempted to cede his title to his younger brother Ding Sheng but fled when his request was ignored. His friend Bao Jun persuaded him to return, citing the importance of upholding his father's legacy. Ding Hong returned, taught disciples, and was later summoned by Emperor Xianzong, becoming a servant and then Captain of Shesheng. He participated in the White Tiger Temple discussions on the Five Classics, where his eloquence was praised. He was promoted to Shaofu and later Taichang. During Empress Dowager Dou's regency, Ding Hong submitted a memorial warning against the Dou family's power, citing solar eclipses as divine warnings. His advice led to the confiscation of Dou Xian's seal and the suicides of Dou Xian and his brothers. Ding Hong also reformed the system for recommending filial and incorrupt candidates. He died in the sixth year of Yongyuan.

Yu Xu, from Wuping in Chen, was known for his integrity. His grandfather, a prison officer, handled cases with compassion. Yu Xu was orphaned young and cared for his grandmother, refusing an official post until after her death. He later served as a doctor. When General Deng Zhi proposed abandoning Liangzhou due to Qiang rebellions, Yu Xu argued against it, stating it would expose the imperial tombs and that Liangzhou's people were a vital defense. He suggested controlling local leaders by giving their sons official posts to prevent rebellion. Deng Zhi, resentful of Yu Xu's opposition, sent him to govern Chaoge, a bandit-ridden area. Yu Xu used deception, recruiting former bandits to ambush others and marking thieves' clothes with silk threads, leading to their dispersal. Promoted to Wudu's prefect, he again used deception against the Qiang, increasing his campfires to feign strength and marching rapidly. He then used a strategy of weak arrows to lure the Qiang into range of his strong crossbows, defeating them. He improved the county by building fortifications, opening waterways for transport, and increasing the population. As Sili Xiaowei, he impeached powerful officials, earning their hatred. He was framed and sentenced to hard labor, but eunuch Sun Cheng defended him, leading to his release and promotion. He later abolished the practice of "righteous money" and argued for fair treatment of petitioners. He remained upright despite nine reprimands and three punishments, dying as Shangshu Ling. On his deathbed, he regretted killing many bandits at Chaoge, believing it brought divine punishment.
Fu Xie, from Lingzhou, was known for his caution in speech and action. He served as Sima under Huangfu Song against Zhang Jiao's Yellow Turbans. Before the campaign, he warned the emperor that the real threat was internal, from eunuchs like Zhao Zhong, and that evil and good cannot coexist. Despite his merits, Zhao Zhong framed him, but the emperor spared him. Later, when Situ Cui Lie proposed abandoning Liangzhou during a Xiqiang rebellion, Fu Xie vehemently opposed him, arguing that Liangzhou was the empire's shield and that abandoning it would empower the barbarians. The emperor agreed. Fu Xie refused to curry favor with the powerful eunuch Zhao Zhong, even when offered a marquisate. As Hanyang's governor, he pacified the Qiang. He warned Governor Geng Bi against attacking Han Sui with untrained troops, predicting disaster. Geng Bi ignored him and was killed. When Hanyang was besieged, Fu Xie refused to abandon the city despite his son's pleas and the offer of safe passage from grateful Hu cavalry. He chose to die in battle, cursing a defecting official. His posthumous title was Zhuangjiehou.
Gai Xun, from Dunhuang, was a Xiaolian and Hanyang's chief historian. He refused to take revenge on an enemy, Su Zhenghe, when the governor wanted to kill him to cover for a corrupt prefect, arguing it was wrong to kill a good man. He later remonstrated with Governor Zuo Chang for embezzling funds, but Zuo Chang sent him to a dangerous post. Gai Xun survived and later rescued Zuo Chang from a siege by Bian Zhang. He criticized Governor Song Xiao's plan to teach the *Classic of Filial Piety* to pacify the border, calling it impractical. During a battle against Qiang rebels, he was wounded but refused to flee, cursing his captors. The Qiang, respecting his courage, released him. As a famine relief official, he used his own grain to save over a thousand people. Summoned by Emperor Ling, he blamed eunuchs for the world's chaos. He planned with Liu Yu and Yuan Shao to kill the eunuchs, but was made Jing Zhaoyin instead. There, he prosecuted a corrupt official despite pleas from nobles. After Emperor Ling's death, he wrote to Dong Zhuo, criticizing his deposition of the young emperor. He openly defied Dong Zhuo in court, refusing to bow. He died of illness at 51, refusing Dong Zhuo's funeral gifts.
Zang Hong, from Guangling, was made a Dong Zilang due to his father's military merits. After Dong Zhuo killed the emperor, Zang Hong urged Prefect Zhang Chao to raise an army. He helped organize an alliance at Suanzao, where he gave a passionate oath, calling for the destruction of Dong Zhuo. The alliance, however, failed to act decisively. Later, Zang Hong served Yuan Shao as Qingzhou's governor, pacifying the region. When Cao Cao besieged Zhang Chao, Zang Hong begged Yuan Shao for troops to rescue him, but Yuan Shao refused. Zhang Chao was killed. Enraged, Zang Hong broke with Yuan Shao, who then besieged him. Despite a letter from Chen Lin urging surrender, Zang Hong refused, accusing Yuan Shao of betraying allies and killing loyal men. He stated he would rather die for righteousness. During the siege, he shared his last food with his soldiers and even killed his concubine to feed them. The city fell, and Zang Hong was captured. He defiantly cursed Yuan Shao for his treachery and was executed. His subordinate Chen Rong also chose to die with him.

Yuan Shao, courtesy name Benchu, was from Ruyang, Runan, and the grandson of Situ Yuan Tang. His father Yuan Cheng served as a lieutenant general. Yuan Shao began his career as a Langguan and later became Chief of Puyang. After his mother's death, he resigned to observe mourning, and later also mourned his father. He then moved to Luoyang, where his elegant demeanor and generosity attracted many scholars, leading to resentment from court eunuchs. His uncle Yuan Wei reprimanded him, but Yuan Shao did not change his ways. Yuan Shao served under General He Jin as a subordinate officer and later as Colonel of the Eight Xiuyuan. After Emperor Ling's death, he advised He Jin to eliminate the eunuchs, but He Jin was killed. When Dong Zhuo arrived, Yuan Shao opposed his plan to depose the young emperor. After a heated argument, Yuan Shao fled to Jizhou. Dong Zhuo initially offered a reward for his capture but later pardoned him and appointed him Governor of Bohai and Marquis of Yunxiang.
In the first year of Chuping, Yuan Shao raised troops in Bohai, joining forces with Yuan Shu, Han Fu, and others to crusade against Dong Zhuo. They formed an alliance with Yuan Shao as leader. Dong Zhuo killed Yuan Shao's uncle and clan members in the capital. Yuan Shao then took control of Jizhou from Han Fu through a combination of military pressure and persuasion, becoming its governor. He appointed Ju Shou as his advisor and expanded his territory.
Yuan Shao defeated Gongsun Zan in battle, killing Yan Gang and pursuing him to the boundary bridge. Despite a near-capture by Gongsun Zan's cavalry, Yuan Shao's forces prevailed. He later suppressed rebellions in Wei County and defeated the Black Mountain bandits, killing tens of thousands. Yuan Shao also killed his general Qu Yi for insubordination.
When Emperor Xian was in danger, Ju Shou advised Yuan Shao to welcome the emperor, but Yuan Shao hesitated due to advice from Guo Tu and Chunyu Qiong. He eventually declined. Yuan Shao had three sons: Yuan Tan, Yuan Xi, and Yuan Shang. He favored Yuan Shang due to his wife's influence, adopting Yuan Tan as his brother's heir and sending him to Qingzhou, against Ju Shou's warnings.
In the first year of Jian'an, Cao Cao welcomed the emperor to Xu County and blamed Yuan Shao for not aiding the emperor. Yuan Shao responded with a lengthy letter defending his actions, citing his loyalty and efforts against Dong Zhuo and others. The court appointed him Taiwei and Marquis of Ye, but he refused until Cao Cao yielded the position of General. Later, he was granted command of four provinces.
Yuan Shao attacked Gongsun Zan again, pacifying Youzhou. With control of four provinces and hundreds of thousands of troops, he grew arrogant. He planned to attack Xu County, ignoring Ju Shou's advice to rest and farm. Instead, he followed Guo Tu and Shen Pei's counsel to attack immediately. Tian Feng's warnings led to his imprisonment.
In the fifth year of Jian'an, Yuan Shao marched south after Liu Bei's defection. He issued a proclamation condemning Cao Cao's crimes. His forces initially succeeded but were defeated at Guandu after Xu You defected and revealed the location of Yuan Shao's grain supplies at Wuchao. Cao Cao attacked and destroyed the supplies, leading to Yuan Shao's defeat. Yuan Shao fled with 800 cavalry, while many of his troops were killed or surrendered. Ju Shou was captured and executed after attempting to return to Yuan Shao.
Yuan Shao appeared generous but was proud and unable to accept advice, leading to his downfall. After his defeat, he killed Tian Feng. He fell ill and died in the seventh year of Jian'an. His succession was disputed: Shen Pei and Feng Ji supported Yuan Shang, while others favored Yuan Tan, leading to internal conflict.

The Xiqiang people, originally from Sanmiao, a branch of the Jiang surname, lived in a region near Nanyue, stretching from the Cizhi River to the borders of Shu and Han in the south and Shanshan and Cheshi in the northwest. They were nomadic, migrating with water and grass, relying primarily on livestock rather than grain. Their society lacked fixed clans, with tribes named after paternal or maternal lines. After twelve generations, intermarriage occurred, and customs included marrying stepmothers after a father's death and widows after an elder brother's death, leading to rapid population growth. They had no central ruler; power determined leadership, with violence and plunder common. Their soldiers excelled in valley combat but not on plains, valued death in battle over illness, and endured harsh conditions.
Historically, the Xiqiang's relationship with Chinese dynasties fluctuated. During the Xia Dynasty, Taikang's loss of control led to barbarian rebellion, but later rulers like Houxiang and Houxie subdued them. Under the Yin Dynasty, Wuding conquered Xirong and Guifang, but Wu Yi's brutality provoked Dog Soldier invasions. The Zhou Dynasty saw King Wen and King Wu command Xirong, while King Mu campaigned against Quanrong. As Zhou weakened, Rong tribes invaded, leading to conflicts with Qin and Jin. During the Spring and Autumn period, Rong groups like Yiqu and Dali grew powerful, building cities and claiming kingship. Qin gradually absorbed them, with King Zhao of Qin destroying Yiqu in the 4th century BCE.
Under the Han Dynasty, the Xiqiang faced expulsion and relocation. Emperor Wu expanded borders, building fortresses and separating Qiang from Xiongnu. In 42 BCE, Xianling Qiang allied with Xiongnu, attacking Lingju and Paohan, but were suppressed by General Li Xi. Later, Zhao Chongguo defeated them in 60 BCE. During Wang Mang's reign, Qiang lands were seized, but after his fall, they rebelled. In 25 CE, Guangwu restored the Qiang Protectorate, but conflicts persisted. Ma Yuan defeated Qiang rebellions in 35 CE, moving them to Tianshui and Longxi. By 58 CE, Dianwu's rebellion was crushed, and Qiang were resettled in Sanfu.
The Qiang continued to resist Han rule. In 77 CE, Miwu led a revolt, defeating Han forces. Fu Yu, the Qiang Protector, was killed in 87 CE. Zhang Yu retaliated by poisoning Qiang leaders, but Miwu's son Mitang continued raids. Deng Xun and later officials used bribery to divide the Qiang, but conflicts resumed. In 107 CE, the Qiang rebellion under Dianling and others devastated border regions, costing billions and causing massive displacement. Ren Shang and Deng Zun campaigned against them, but corruption and mismanagement plagued efforts. By 118 CE, the Qiang were largely subdued, though sporadic revolts occurred.
In later years, the Qiang faced further suppression. Ma Xian defeated them in 141 CE, but his death in battle in 144 CE led to renewed chaos. Zhao Chong and others campaigned, but the Qiang declined by the 2nd century CE. During the Han dynasty's decline, Qiang allied with Yellow Turban rebels in 184 CE. By the 3rd century CE, the Qiang had fragmented into 150 tribes, with the Zhong Qiang being the most powerful, fielding over 100,000 warriors. The Yuezhi Hu, a related group, intermarried with Qiang and lived in Huangzhong. The text concludes that the Qiang's persistent harm stemmed from Han mismanagement, including broken promises and exploitation. The Yongchu period saw widespread rebellion, with Qiang plundering Sanfu and cutting off Longxi. Despite costly campaigns by generals like Deng Lu and Ren Shang, the Han failed to achieve lasting peace. The author criticizes the policy of relocating Qiang into Han territory, which exacerbated conflicts. Ultimately, the Qiang were suppressed by Duan Yi, but the Han dynasty's decline followed. The narrative emphasizes the cyclical nature of Qiang-Han relations, marked by rebellion, suppression, and eventual fragmentation.

Guo Ji, from Maoling, Fufeng, was born into a family with a knightly ancestor and a prefect father. During the reigns of Emperor Ai and Emperor Ping, he served in the Da Sikong Mansion and became Yuyang Duwei. Under Wang Mang, he was Great Yin of Shanggu. During the Gengshi era, when the three auxiliaries were invaded, Gengshi appointed him Zuo Fengyi to pacify the people. After Shizu ascended, Guo Ji became Yongzhou's pastor and later a minister offering loyal advice. In the fourth year of Jianwu, he became prefect of Zhongshan, then governor of Yuyang after Peng Chong's defeat. There, he eliminated bandits through punishment and reward, and organized defenses against the Xiongnu, who ceased border incursions. After five years, household registrations doubled. In the ninth year, he became prefect of Yingchuan to suppress bandits, successfully recruiting Zhao Hong and Zhao Wu to surrender. Later appointed Bingzhou pastor, he advised selecting officials from worthy candidates nationwide rather than exclusively from Nanyang. He was known for keeping promises to children who welcomed him on horseback. He served long in Bingzhou due to Lu Fang's troubles, eventually forcing Lu Fang to flee to the Xiongnu. He resigned due to age and illness, became Taizhong doctor, distributed his wealth among his clan, and died at eighty-six.
Du Shi, from Ji County, Hanoi, was talented from youth. He served as a county meritorious official, then joined the Da Sima Mansion. In the first year of Jianwu, he became Shi Yushi and executed the violent General Xiao Guang, receiving ceremonial halberds from Liu Xiu. He later killed the traitor Yang Yi and others. As magistrate of Chenggao, then captain of Pei and Runan, he governed well. In the seventh year, he became Nanyang Prefect, known for frugality and honesty. He invented a water-powered piston bellows for iron smelting, making agricultural tools more efficiently. He repaired ponds and expanded farmland, enriching the county. People compared him to former prefect Zhao Xinchen. Feeling uneasy about his merit, he requested demotion, arguing that troops needed rest and that meritorious generals should be rewarded with county positions. The emperor refused. Du Shi recommended talented people and proposed using tiger talismans for troop mobilization to prevent forgery, which the emperor accepted. After seven years, he was recalled due to a case involving his brother's revenge. He died poor without land or house; the emperor provided funeral expenses.
Kong Fen, from Maoling, Fufeng, studied the Zuo Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals under Liu Xin. During Wang Mang's rebellion, he fled to Hexi with his mother and brother. In the fifth year of Jianwu, Dou Rong appointed him as chief aunt. He became Marquis of Guannei. Despite Guzang's wealth, Kong Fen's property did not increase in four years. He served his mother filially, eating vegetables with his wife while others laughed at his frugality. After Long and Shu were pacified, when other Hexi governors left with满载 goods, Kong Fen rode alone with nothing. The people offered him cattle, horses, and utensils worth over ten million, but he accepted nothing. In the capital, he became Commander of Wudu. When thieves captured his wife and son as hostages, he pursued relentlessly, resulting in their deaths. The emperor commended him and made him prefect of Wudu, where he governed with clarity. He resigned due to illness and died at home. His younger brother Kong Qi and son Kong Jia both wrote works on the Zuo Commentary.
Zhang Kan, from Wan, Nanyang, was orphaned early and shared his father's wealth with his brother and son. At sixteen, he studied in Chang'an, where classmates called him "Holy Boy." Shizu praised him early on. After ascending, the emperor appointed him as an official. He delivered silk and horses to Wu Han for attacking Gongsun Shu, becoming prefect of Shu County. When the Han army had only seven days of food and planned retreat, Zhang Kan persuaded Wu Han to stay, leading to Gongsun Shu's defeat. After capturing Chengdu, Zhang Kan inspected the treasury without taking anything. He comforted the people, who were delighted. Later, as Governor of Yuyang, he defeated a Xiongnu invasion of 10,000 cavalry with only 1,000 horsemen. He opened over 8,000 hectares of rice fields, enriching the county. The people sang his praises. After eight years, the Xiongnu dared not invade. A Shu County commander testified that when Gongsun Shu was defeated, Zhang Kan left with only a quilt bag despite mountains of treasure.
Lian Fan, from Duling, was a descendant of Zhao general Lian Po. His family had served as frontier county guards for generations. After his father died in Shu Han, fifteen-year-old Lian Fan went to retrieve his body. The prefect offered money, which he refused. When the coffin boat sank, Lian Fan clung to it and was rescued. He studied under Dr. Xue Han. When Xue Han was killed for involvement in King Chu Ying's rebellion, Lian Fan alone collected his body. The emperor questioned him but pardoned him for his courage. As governor of Yunzhong, when the Huns invaded with overwhelming numbers, Lian Fan ordered soldiers to light multiple torches, making the enemy think reinforcements had arrived. He pursued at dawn, killing hundreds. The Huns never attacked Yunzhong again. As prefect of Shu County, he discouraged frivolous debate and abolished night work restrictions, instead requiring water storage for fire prevention. The people sang his praises. He was known for generosity, once giving his horse to a mourning official without revealing his identity. He died at home.
Wang Tang, from Guanghan, was promoted from county magistrate due to his governance. During Yongchu, when Western Qiang rebels troubled Ba County, Wang Tang became prefect, killed over a thousand Qiang captives, and pacified the region. The people built a shrine for him. As You Fufeng, he refused to accommodate the powerful wet nurse Wang Sheng and eunuch Jiang Jing during Emperor An's western expedition, closing his gate to them. Falsely accused, he was vindicated after the emperor's death and Jiang Jing's execution. He later served as Prime Minister of Lu, then prefect of Runan, where he delegated authority to capable subordinates like Chen Fan and Ying Si, achieving good governance. He was hated by General Liang Shang and Minister Yuan Tang, who falsely accused him and had him dismissed. He died at eighty-six, requesting a simple burial.

Liu Yi criticized the nine-rank Zhongzheng system, listing eight drawbacks: it relied on personal connections, ignored true talent, caused disputes, and led to corruption. He argued it failed to select virtuous officials and advocated for its abolition. The emperor did not implement his proposal. Liu Yi was dedicated to public service, speaking sincerely, and was respected by all. He was strict with his family, punishing his wife for visiting him during a fast. Despite his poverty, the emperor rewarded him generously. At seventy, he retired but was later recommended as Qingzhou's Grand Central Magistrate, though some officials opposed it. Sun Yin argued for his appointment, citing his integrity and ability. Liu Yi died in the sixth year of Taikang, and the emperor mourned him deeply, posthumously honoring him.
Liu Yi's son, Liu Tun, inherited his father's integrity. He served as a doctor and was punished for opposing the emperor's will. Later, he became Suanzao Ling and Shi Yushi, impeaching Wang Hun for misconduct. Liu Tun also criticized Guo Zhang for failing to put out a fire, causing Guo to reform. He served as Taiyuan's internal history, refused to serve under King Sima Lun, and participated in the three kings' revolt. He was appointed as Zuocheng and censor Zhongcheng, impeaching many officials. He was knighted for his role in attacking Sima Tong but dismissed after Sima Yi's death. He later served as Sili school lieutenant again, defending Queen Yang against King Sima Yong. He fled to Sima Lue and helped repel Liu Gen. After the emperor's return, he was honored but later killed by Shi Le's patrol cavalry.
Other figures include Cheng Wei, a strict official recruited by Liu Yi; He Xiao, a capable administrator praised for his integrity; Wu Yi, a perceptive official who criticized figures; Ren Kai, a loyal minister who opposed Jia Chong and was slandered; Cui Hong, a stern censor who punished misconduct; Guo Yi, a magnanimous official who recognized talent; Hou Shiguang, a loyal and frugal minister; and He Pan, a fair-minded official who helped clear injustices. The text concludes with a commentary praising these officials for their integrity and service, despite facing challenges and slander.
