Jiang Yan, courtesy name Wentong, was a native of Kaocheng, Jiyang. He was lonely and impoverished in his youth but diligent, studious, and reserved. He began his official career as an appointee in Southern Xuzhou and later served at the imperial court. He followed Prince Jingsu of Song Jianping to southern Yanzhou. When Guangling Magistrate Guo Yanwen was convicted, Jiang Yan was imprisoned. From prison, he wrote a letter to Jingsu, pleading his innocence and loyalty, citing historical examples of unjust suffering. He described his humble origins and sincere service, lamenting that slander had led to his imprisonment. He begged for mercy, and Jingsu, moved by the letter, released him that day.
Jiang Yan was soon promoted and served in various posts, including as a scholar in Southern Xuzhou and Zuo Changshi of Baling Kingdom. When Jingsu became governor of Jingzhou, Jiang Yan followed him. As Jingsu grew arrogant and plotted rebellion, Jiang Yan repeatedly advised him against it, warning of historical disasters. Jingsu ignored him. When Jingsu was stationed in Beijing, Jiang Yan served in the army and governed Nandonghai. He wrote fifteen poems to satirize Jingsu’s schemes. After a dispute over county governance, Jingsu had Jiang Yan demoted to Jian'an Wuxingling, where he served for three years.
When Qi Yi came to power, he recruited Jiang Yan as Shangshu Jiabulang. During Shen Youzhi’s rebellion, Emperor Gao consulted Jiang Yan, who analyzed the strengths of the emperor and the weaknesses of the rebels, predicting victory. Emperor Gao was pleased and entrusted Jiang Yan with drafting military documents. Jiang Yan held numerous high offices under Qi, including Hussar Yuzhang Wang Ji's Office, Vice Minister of Zhongshu, and General Xiaoqi. He served as governor of Luling and later returned to the capital as General of Cavalry and Minister Zuocheng. As Censor Zhongcheng, he impeached several officials for negligence and corruption, earning praise from Emperor Ming for his strictness.
Under Emperor Ming, Jiang Yan held positions such as Chief Historian of the Chariot and Linhai King, Shizhong, and Prefect of Xuancheng. During the Yongyuan period, when Cui Huijing besieged the capital, Jiang Yan feigned illness and avoided the rebels, earning admiration for his foresight. He later served as Secretary Supervisor and Guard, though he felt unqualified. He was enfeoffed as Founding Uncle of Linju County. In his later years, he expressed contentment and a desire to retire. He died at age sixty-two, and the emperor mourned him with gifts. Jiang Yan was known for his literary talent in youth but declined in later years. He authored over a hundred works and ten records of "History of Qi."
Ren Fang, courtesy name Yansheng, was a native of Bochang, Le'an. His father was Yao, a doctor of Zhongsan in Qi. Ren Fang was studious and became famous early. At sixteen, he served as chief bookkeeper for Song Danyang Yin Liu Bing. He later held various posts, including Dr. Taichang and chief secretary for Wang Jian. Ren Fang was known for his filial piety, mourning his parents with extreme devotion. He served as a defense officer and secretary of Guan Dong Palace. During Qi Mingdi’s reign, he drafted a memorial declining high honors, citing his inadequacy and the state’s troubles. His refusal angered the emperor, stalling his career.
Ren Fang excelled in writing essays, biographies, and memorials, often composing without revision. He was admired by contemporaries like Xuan. After the dynasty’s fall, he served under Liang, holding posts such as Huangmen Shilang and Minister of Personnel. As governor of Yixing, he lived frugally, eating only wheat. He died in office at age forty-nine, and the people built a shrine for him. The emperor mourned deeply. Ren Fang was generous with friends, recommending scholars and hosting many guests. He was called "Renjun" for his patronage. Despite poverty, he accumulated over ten thousand books. After his death, the emperor took rare books from his collection. Ren Fang’s writings totaled hundreds of thousands of words. However, after his death, his children were neglected. Liu Xiaobiao wrote an essay criticizing fair-weather friends, describing five types of snobbish acquaintances: those drawn to power, wealth, reputation, shared misfortune, and calculated gain. He lamented that Ren Fang’s former friends abandoned his family.
Yao Cha commented that Jiang Yan and Ren Fang were talented writers of their time. Jiang Yan’s calm and cautious nature allowed him to maintain his reputation, though he relied on prior connections. Ren Fang’s works included 247 volumes of "Miscellaneous Biography," 252 volumes of "Diji," and 33 volumes of articles. His son Seri resembled him and served as Shangshu Waibinglang.

Fu Manrong, from Anqiu, lost his father early and lived with his mother and brother in the South China Sea. He was studious, proficient in Laozi and the Book of Changes, and bold in speech. He gathered students to teach and held various official positions, including Piaoqi Canjun and Nanhai Prefect. During the Qi Dynasty, he served as Tongzhi Sanqi Changshi and later as Zhongshu Lang. He was known for lecturing on scriptures at home, attracting dozens or hundreds of students. In the Liang Dynasty, he was appointed as Sima and Linhai Prefect, dying at eighty-two. He authored annotations on the Zhouyi, Mao's Poems, and other works. Yao Cha noted that these scholars, despite varying fortunes, contributed to Confucian learning during the Liang Dynasty.
He Tongzhi, from Lujiang, was deeply interested in the Three Rites from childhood, studying independently and mastering three hundred chapters of the Li. Respected by Taiwei Wang Jian, he held various posts, including Shangshu Temple Minister and Infantry Colonel. During the Yongyuan period, despite war, he continued lecturing. After Emperor Gaozu's ascension, he became Zuocheng, aiding in system creation. He died at fifty-five, posthumously honored as Huangmen Shilang. He wrote about one hundred articles on Li Yi. Fan Zhen, from Nanxiang, lost his father young and served his mother filially. He studied under Liu Shan, excelling in the Three Rites. He served as an envoy to the Wei and was known for his straightforward nature. He debated Buddhism with Xiao Ziliang, arguing against the existence of gods. His "Theory on the Destruction of Gods" sparked controversy. He held various posts, including Yidu Prefect and Jin'an Prefect, dying as Zhongshu Lang. His son Fan Xu inherited his knowledge. Confucius Qu, from Kuaiji, lost his father young but became proficient in the Guwen Shangshu. He served as a lecturer and helped compile the Liang Guan. He died at fifty-one, authoring works on the Shangshu.
Yan Zhizhi, from Jianping, was proficient in Zhuangzi, Laozi, and the Three Rites. He served as Luling Kingdom Minister and Guanghan Kingdom Right Changshi, known for his righteousness in handling the Guanghan King's funeral. He was appointed as a Five Classics doctor, lecturing to hundreds of students. He died at fifty-two, leaving his family in poverty. He authored 479 volumes of Annotations on Evil Etiquette.
He Chang, from Kuaiji, inherited family education in the Three Rites. Recommended by Liu Xian, he served as Taichang Cheng and Five Classics doctor, lecturing on the Li. He authored works on etiquette and the Five Classics, dying at fifty-nine. His son He Ge also became a renowned scholar, lecturing on the Three Rites.
Sima Yun, from Hanoi, lost his father young but loved learning, excelling in the Three Rites. He served as Shangshu Temple Minister and debated mourning rites for loving mothers. He died as Shixing Neishi. His son Sima Shou inherited his studies. Bian Hua, from Jiyin, lost his father young but studied the Five Classics, especially the Book of Changes. He served as a Five Classics doctor, known for his eloquence and musical expertise. He died as Wuling Prefect. Cui Lingen, from Qinghe, studied the Five Classics, especially the Three Rites and Three Commentaries. He served as Taichang Doctor in the Northern Dynasties before returning to Liang, where he lectured to hundreds. He authored numerous works on the classics. Kong Qian, from Kuaiji, studied under He Yin, excelling in the Five Classics. He served as a Five Classics doctor but was not skilled in governance. He died during the Liqian turmoil.
Lu Guang, from Fanyang, was proficient in scriptures and served as a Five Classics doctor, known for his clear pronunciation. He died as Xunyang Prefect.
Shen Jun, from Wuxing, studied the Five Classics, especially the Three Rites. Recommended as a Five Classics doctor, he lectured to hundreds. He died as Wukang Ling. Taishi Shuming, from Wuxing, was proficient in Zhuangzi, Laozi, and the Book of Changes, lecturing to over five hundred. He died at seventy-three.
Huang Kan, from Wu County, studied under He Chang, excelling in the Three Rites. He lectured to hundreds and authored the Book of Rites. He died at fifty-eight.

Queen Xiaoyuan was the aunt of Wang Mang, who claimed descent from the Yellow Emperor. According to Wang Mang's autobiography "Ziben," the lineage traced from the Yellow Emperor through Yu Shun to various descendants who were granted titles during the Zhou Dynasty. The family eventually took the surname Wang after Tian An, a descendant of Qi royalty, lost his feudal state during the Han Dynasty and was called "Wang Family" by the people of Qi. Wang Mang's ancestor Wang He (Wengru) served as Emperor Wu's embroidered censor. Unlike other harsh officials who killed tens of thousands, Wengru showed leniency and was dismissed for not following the emperor's wishes. He saved over ten thousand people and predicted his descendants would prosper. After resigning, he moved to Yuancheng in Wei County, where a divination predicted that a virtuous woman would appear in 645 years, and later that the Wang family would have a noble daughter who would flourish.
Wengru's son Wang Jin fathered Wang Zhengjun, who became Empress of Emperor Yuan. Before her birth, her mother dreamed of the moon falling into her belly. Zhengjun was gentle and virtuous. After two betrothals ended with her fiancés dying, a fortune-teller declared her extremely valuable. She entered the palace at eighteen and became pregnant after being summoned by the crown prince, giving birth to Emperor Cheng. When Emperor Yuan considered deposing the prince due to his fondness for King Dingtao Gong, Wang Feng (the queen's brother) worried alongside the queen. Emperor Yuan ultimately did not depose the prince due to the queen's caution and the late emperor's regard for him. After Emperor Yuan's death, Emperor Cheng ascended, honoring his mother as Empress Dowager and appointing Wang Feng as Grand General. The Wang family's prosperity began, with five brothers granted marquisates on the same day, known as the Five Marquises.
Wang Feng held immense power, with Emperor Cheng afraid to act independently. When Emperor Cheng wanted to appoint Liu Xin as a regular attendant, he was told to ask Wang Feng first, who refused. Emperor Cheng had no choice but to give up. Wang Feng dominated all state affairs, and ministers dared not look directly at him.
After Wang Feng's death, Wang Yin succeeded him as Grand Sima, followed by Wang Shang and Wang Gen. The Wang family's extravagance was legendary, with concubines, slaves, and lavish palaces. The common people sang songs comparing their palaces to the emperor's White Tiger Palace. Despite their excesses, they cultivated wise men to appear refined.
Emperor Cheng had no heirs for over twenty years. King Dingtao's grandmother bribed Wang Gen to make him crown prince. After Emperor Cheng's death, Emperor Ai ascended but was unhappy with the Wang family's power. He eventually forced Wang Mang and others to return to their fiefdoms. When Emperor Ai died without an heir, the Empress Dowager appointed Wang Mang as Grand Sima, and they installed Emperor Ping, who was only nine years old.
Wang Mang gradually consolidated power, eventually becoming regent and later usurping the throne to establish the Xin dynasty. The Empress Dowager refused to give him the imperial seal, angrily denouncing him for betraying the Han dynasty. She threw the seal on the ground, predicting the Wang family would be exterminated. Wang Mang changed her title to "New Empress Dowager Wenmu," severing her connection to Han. She died at eighty-four, and ten years later, Han soldiers killed Wang Mang.
The historian Ban Biao noted that since the Three Dynasties, few dynasties fell due to favored women. The Wang family's rise came through four generations of empresses, with five generals and ten marquises, culminating in Wang Mang's usurpation. The Yuan Empress Dowager's loyalty, holding the imperial seal and refusing to surrender it, was truly pitiful.

Gongsun He, a native of Beidi Commandery, rose from a knight-errant background through military merit. He became favored due to his marriage to Empress Wei's sister and served as a general under Emperor Wu, earning the title of Marquis of Nanao for attacking the Xiongnu. After losing his marquisate for presenting inferior gold, he eventually became Chancellor and was titled Marquis of Ge Yi. He reluctantly accepted the position, weeping and predicting his own danger. His son Gongsun Jingsheng, arrogant and corrupt, embezzled military funds. To atone for his son, Gongsun He captured the knight Zhu Anshi, who retaliated by reporting Gongsun Jingsheng's affair with a princess and accusations of witchcraft against the emperor. Both father and son died in prison, and their clan was exterminated. This incident sparked the witchcraft disaster that ultimately led to the deaths of the princess, empress, and crown prince.
Liu Quli, son of Prince Jing of Zhongshan, replaced Gongsun He as Left Chancellor. Emperor Wu issued an edict condemning Gongsun He's corruption and appointed Liu Quli as Marquis of Peng. During the witchcraft rebellion, Crown Prince Ju killed the accuser Jiang Chong and raised troops. Liu Quli led imperial forces against the prince, resulting in a five-day battle with tens of thousands dead. The prince fled but was captured twenty days later. The following year, Liu Quli conspired with General Li Guangli to make the Prince of Changyi crown prince. This conspiracy was discovered, and Liu Quli was executed by waist-cutting, while Li Guangli surrendered to the Xiongnu. Che Qianqiu, originally named Tian, served as guardian of Emperor Gaozu's tomb. After the crown prince's defeat, Che submitted a memorial defending the prince, arguing that a son who mobilizes troops against his father should only be whipped. Emperor Wu, already regretting his actions, was moved and appointed Che as Grand Herald, then Chancellor within months, creating the unprecedented precedent of becoming Chancellor through a single memorial. Though lacking scholarly talents, Che proved competent and kind-hearted. After Emperor Wu's death, Che served under Emperor Zhao alongside General Huo Guang, deferring to Huo's authority while maintaining loyalty. He served as Chancellor for twelve years and was posthumously titled Marquis Ding.
Wang Xin of Jinan Commandery rose from minor official to magistrate. When Imperial Censor Bao Shengzhi investigated and prepared to execute him, Wang Xin pleaded for mercy, arguing that killing him would not increase Shengzhi's prestige. Impressed, Shengzhi spared him and later recommended him. Wang Xin served Emperor Wu competently, becoming You Fufeng. Under Emperor Zhao, he succeeded Che Qianqiu as Chancellor and was titled Marquis of Yichun, dying the following year.
Yang Chang of Huayin Commandery served in General Huo Guang's staff, rising to Minister of Agriculture. Learning of a rebellion conspiracy, Yang Chang, being cautious, feigned illness rather than reporting it. Another official reported the matter and received a marquisate, while Yang Chang was denied this honor. He later became Imperial Censor and succeeded Wang Xin as Chancellor, titled Marquis of Anping. After Emperor Zhao's death, when Huo Guang planned to depose the immoral King of Changyi, Yang Chang initially hesitated but was persuaded by his wife to cooperate. He died shortly after Emperor Xuan's accession.

Wei Qing, courtesy name Zhongqing, was the illegitimate son of Zheng Ji, a county official in Pingyang, and a servant named Wei. He assumed the surname Wei after his sister Wei Zifu gained favor with Emperor Wu. As a youth, Wei Qing herded sheep and was treated poorly by his relatives. A prisoner once prophesied he would become a marquis, but Wei Qing dismissed this, content to avoid beatings. He later became a knight for the Pingyang Hou family. Wei Zifu's entry into the palace and pregnancy provoked jealousy from Empress Chen and her mother, the Grand Princess, who imprisoned Wei Qing. His friend Gongsun Ao rescued him, and the emperor subsequently appointed Wei Qing as a eunuch and minister. His rise brought wealth to his family. Fan Kuai, a native of Peixian County, was a dog butcher by trade. He hid with Emperor Gaozu in the Mangshan and Cishan areas to avoid official duties. During Chen Sheng's uprising, Xiao He and Cao Shen sent Fan Kuai to retrieve Gaozu, who became Peigong. Fan Kuai served as a Sheren, attacking Huling, Fangyu, and Fengyi, defeating the Sishui County Supervisor. He pacified Peixian County and defeated the Sishui County Governor at Xuexian. He fought Sima Chao in Ci County, beheading fifteen enemies, earning the title of doctor. Fan Kuai frequently followed Peigong, leading assaults on Puyang, Chengyang, and Hufu, beheading many enemies and receiving promotions. He fought at Chengwu, Boyi, Gangli, and Kaifeng, beheading a commander and sixty-eight enemies, earning the title of minister. He defeated Yang Xiong at Quyu, ascended Wanling first, and was named Xianchengjun. He fought at Changshe, Nianyuan, and the Yellow River ferry, defeating Qin forces at Xixiang and Nianyi. He defeated Nanyang's Shouling at Yangcheng, ascended Wancheng first, and repelled enemies at Li County. At Wuguan and Bashang, he beheaded a captain and ten enemies, capturing 146 and surrendering 2,900 soldiers.
At the Hongmen Banquet, Xiang Yu prepared to attack Peigong. Peigong apologized to Xiang Yu via Xiang Bo. During the feast, Yafu ordered Xiang Zhuang to assassinate Peigong with a sword dance, but Xiang Bo protected him. Fan Kuai, hearing the urgency, entered the camp with sword and shield, confronting Xiang Yu. He drank wine and ate pork leg, condemning Xiang Yu for listening to slander and estranging Peigong. Xiang Yu remained silent. Peigong left, and Fan Kuai escorted him back to Bashang, leaving Zhang Liang to apologize. Xiang Yu abandoned his plan to kill Peigong. Later, Xiang Yu entered Xianyang, burning and killing, and made Peigong King of Han. Fan Kuai was made Marquis of Linwu, then doctor, and followed the king to Hanzhong. He pacified the Three Qin Dynasties, attacking Xixian, Yong County, Yongxian, and Tengcheng, ascending cities first. He attacked Zhang Ping at Haozhi, beheading a magistrate and a deputy, and was promoted to Cavalry General. He defeated Qin chariot and cavalry forces at Shumian and Rangxiang, becoming a general. He attacked Zhao Bi, occupying Jun, Huaili, Liuzhong, and Xianyang, diverting water to irrigate waste hills. The King of Han granted him Fan Township in Du County as a food town.
Fan Kuai followed the king to attack Xiang Yu, slaughtering Zaoyi and defeating Wang Wu and Cheng Chu at Waihuang. He attacked Zouxian, Luxian, Xiaqiu, and Xuexian. After Xiang Yu defeated the king at Pengcheng, Fan Kuai returned to Rongyang, receiving 2,000 households in Pingyin and garrisoning Guangwu Mountain for a year. He surrounded Xiang Yu at Chen County, defeating him and bloodbathing Hu Ling. After Xiang Yu's death, the king became emperor, granting Fan Kuai 800 households. He followed Gaozu to suppress Zang Tu's rebellion, capturing Zang Tu and pacifying Yan. He arrested Han Xin at Chen County, pacifying Chu. Gaozu granted Fan Kuai the title of Marquis of Wuyang, exempting previous titles. He followed Gaozu to attack Chen Xi in Daidi, pacifying Dai land and increasing households by 1,500. He attacked Chen Xi and Manqiuchen, capturing Bairen County, ascending cities first, and pacifying Qinghe and Changshan counties (27 total), destroying Shuyuan County, and becoming Left Prime Minister. He defeated Qi Muyin and Yin Pan at Wuzhong and Guangchang, and Chen Xi's general Wang Huang at Daidi, attacking Han Xin at Shenhe. His men killed Han Xin, defeated Xiongnu cavalry at Henggu, and captured General Zhao Ji, Prime Minister Feng Liang, and others. He pacified 72 counties in Dai. He attacked Lu Wan, pacifying 18 counties and 51 townships in Yan. Gaozu added 1,300 households, totaling 5,400 in Wuyang. Fan Kuai beheaded 176 enemies, captured 287, defeated seven armies, occupied five cities, and pacified six commanderies and 52 counties. He married Empress Lu's sister, Lu Xu, and had a son, Fan Kang. He was closest to the emperor.

Xiao He, from Peidi, began his career as a meticulous official under Pei Lord, supporting the future Emperor Gaozu (then a commoner and later a pavilion chief) in official matters. When Gaozu served in Xianyang, Xiao He contributed 500 yuan for his farewell, exceeding the 300 yuan given by others. As an official in Sishui County, he excelled in inspections, but declined a court recruitment to remain. When Gaozu rose as Duke of Pei, Xiao He became his prime minister and governor. Upon entering Xianyang, while others seized gold and silk, Xiao He collected Qin’s legal and administrative books, enabling Gaozu to understand the empire’s geography, households, and people’s grievances. As prime minister, he governed Ba and Shu, pacifying the people and supplying the army. In the second year of the Han Dynasty, Xiao He stayed in Guanzhong, governing Yueyang, establishing laws, temples, and counties, reporting to the emperor when possible. He recruited soldiers and supplied grain, earning the emperor’s trust. During the confrontation with Xiang Yu, the emperor’s frequent consolations led Bao Sheng to advise Xiao He to send his capable relatives to the army to allay suspicion, which he did, pleasing the emperor. After Xiang Yu’s death, Liu Bang ascended the throne and awarded Xiao He first among the marquises, granting him 8,000 households. When ministers protested, the emperor compared their merit to hunting dogs and Xiao He’s to a hunter, silencing them. Later, Eqiu argued Xiao He’s contributions—preserving Guanzhong and supplying troops—were eternal, securing him the top rank. Xiao He was granted special court privileges.
During Chen Xi and Han Xin’s rebellions, Xiao He helped Empress Lu kill Han Xin. The emperor granted him 5,000 households and a guard, but Zhao Ping warned this was due to suspicion, advising Xiao He to refuse the reward and fund the army. He complied, pleasing the emperor. When Yingbu rebelled, a retainer warned Xiao He’s popularity could lead to his extermination, urging him to damage his reputation by buying land cheaply. He did so, and the emperor was happy. Later, the emperor imprisoned Xiao He for requesting Linyuan for the people, but a courtier argued his loyalty, leading to his release. Xiao He served Emperor Hui, recommending Cao Shen as his successor. He died in the second year of Xiaohui’s reign, posthumously named Wen Zhonghou. His descendants inherited his title, with later emperors restoring it after extinctions. The praise notes that both Xiao He and Cao Shen, born in Qin, rose with Han, stabilizing the state through their complementary roles—Xiao He guarding Guanzhong and Cao Shen leading expeditions. Their reputations endured, benefiting future generations.
Cao Shen, also from Peidi, served as a jailer in Qin and followed Gaozu as Zhongjuan. He achieved numerous military victories, including defeating Qin forces, capturing cities, and killing generals. After Xiang Yu made Peigong King of Han, Cao Shen became Marquis of Jiancheng. He pacified the Three Qin Dynasties, captured Xianyang, and fought in key battles. As a general and lieutenant, he attacked princes, and after King Xiang’s defeat, he served as false prime minister, defeating Wei and capturing King Bao. He followed Han Xin to attack Zhao and Qi, capturing cities and generals. After the Han emperor’s ascension, Cao Shen became prime minister of Qi, attacking Chen Xi and Yingbu. His achievements included conquering two countries and 122 counties, capturing two kings and three prime ministers.
As prime minister of Qi, Cao Shen adopted Huang-Lao principles, governing with tranquility and earning praise. Upon hearing of Xiao He’s death, he prepared to become prime minister of the court, advising his successor to prioritize prison litigation and market trade. Despite past conflicts, Xiao He recommended Cao Shen. As prime minister, Cao Shen adhered to Xiao He’s laws, selecting loyal elders and excluding those seeking fame. He drank daily, avoiding advice, and covered minor mistakes. When Emperor Hui criticized his inaction, Cao Shen argued that Emperor Gao and Xiao He had established clear laws, and he merely maintained them, which the emperor accepted. He died after three years as prime minister, posthumously named Yihou. His descendants inherited his title, with later generations continuing until Wang Mang’s era.

Zhao Guanghan, a native of Zhuo Commandery, began his career as a county and commandery official, known for his integrity and talent. He was elected as Maocai and served as a market price regulator before becoming the magistrate of Yangdi. His exceptional governance led to his promotion to Lieutenant of Jingfu and acting Jing Zhaoyin. After Emperor Zhao's death, he executed the corrupt Du Jian despite powerful intercessions, earning praise from the capital. He participated in deposing King Changyi and establishing Emperor Xuan, receiving the title of Marquis of Guannei. As Governor of Yingchuan, he suppressed the powerful Yuan and Chu clans and used innovative methods like the "snitch bucket" to break up local factions, restoring order. His reputation spread even to the Xiongnu.
As Jing Zhaoyin, Guanghan was diligent and generous, attributing successes to his subordinates. He was skilled in the "hook distance" method of investigation, uncovering crimes with precision. He once prevented a kidnapping by negotiating with the kidnappers and later treated them with dignity before their execution. He also exposed private affairs with uncanny accuracy, such as knowing a pavilion chief's message before it was delivered. He increased the salary of traveling wardens to prevent corruption, leading to a well-governed capital. However, after General Huo Guang's death, Guanghan raided his son's residence, offending the queen and powerful relatives. He eventually fell from favor after a series of conflicts, including a false accusation against the prime minister's wife. Despite his integrity and popularity among the people, he was executed by waist-cutting.
Yin Wenggui, from Hedong, lost his father early and worked as a prison clerk. As a market official, he curbed the violence of Huo Guang's retainers. Governor Tian Yannian recognized his talent and appointed him to oversee half of the commandery's counties. He later served as Governor of Donghai, where he maintained detailed records of officials' conduct and arrested criminals during official meetings, instilling fear. He executed the cunning Xu Zhongsun, pacifying the region. As You Fufeng, he continued his strict governance, targeting the powerful while being lenient with the weak. He was known for his integrity and modesty, dying in office with no surplus property. The emperor praised him and granted gold to his family.
Han Yanshou, from Handi, was promoted after his father died admonishing King Yan. As Governor of Yingchuan, he replaced Zhao Guanghan's confrontational methods with education in rites, consulting local elders and standardizing ceremonies. The people followed his teachings, abandoning lavish funerals. He later governed Shujun, hiring local worthies and promoting filial piety. He treated officials with kindness, blaming himself for their failures. As Zuo Fengyi, he resolved a land dispute by blaming himself, leading to the brothers' reconciliation. However, he was impeached for exceeding his authority and executed, despite public mourning. His sons resigned from office as he advised.
Zhang Chang, from Hedong, gained fame for admonishing King Changyi. He warned Emperor Xuan about the Huo family's power, advocating for their removal. As Governor of Shanyang, he requested to suppress bandits in Bohai, using rewards and amnesty to disperse them. He also advised the Empress Dowager to stop hunting. As Jing Zhaoyin, he recruited thief leaders to capture others, arresting hundreds in one day. He was known for his wit and leniency, but his frivolous behavior, like thrushing his wife's eyebrows, drew criticism. He served for nine years but was dismissed after killing a subordinate. He later governed Jizhou and Taiyuan, dying of illness. His brother Zhang Wu also governed Liang effectively. Wang Zun, from Zhuo Commandery, began as a prison clerk and studied the classics. As magistrate of Guo County, he executed an unfilial son by shooting. As Governor of Anding, he issued strict notices and killed the corrupt Zhang Fu, shocking the commandery. He was dismissed for excessive killings but later served as Governor of Yizhou, famously scolding his horse at a dangerous pass. As Prime Minister of Dongping, he confronted the arrogant king, who eventually avoided him. He impeached Prime Minister Kuang Heng for misconduct but was demoted. As Jing Zhaoyin, he eliminated bandits in Nanshan and executed powerful criminals, but was dismissed again. He later prevented a Yellow River flood by personally staying on the embankment, earning a promotion. He died in office, remembered by the people.
Wang Zhang, from Taishan, was a blunt admonisher who slandered Zhongshu Ling Shi Xian, leading to his dismissal. Recalled by Emperor Cheng, he became Sili Xiaowei and later Jing Zhaoyin. He accused General Wang Feng of monopolizing power, leading to his execution for treason despite his wife's warnings. His family was exiled but later returned. He served for two years and was mourned by the people. The text concludes that Zhao Guanghan, Han Yanshou, Yin Wenggui, Zhang Chang, Wang Zun, and Wang Zhang were notable officials, though some met tragic ends due to their integrity or conflicts with power.

Li Shiqi of Gaoyang was a learned man from a poor family who worked as a village gatekeeper. When various rebel generals passed through Gaoyang during the uprisings against Qin, he hid from them, considering them narrow-minded. Upon hearing that Pei Gong (later Emperor Gaozu of Han) was far-sighted, Li Shiqi arranged an introduction through a fellow villager serving under Pei Gong. Despite Pei Gong's disdain for Confucian scholars, Li Shiqi boldly criticized him for washing his feet while receiving visitors. Pei Gong apologized, and Li Shiqi advised him to seize Chenliu County, which had abundant food stores. Li Shiqi persuaded the magistrate to surrender, and Pei Gong captured Chenliu, granting Li Shiqi the title of Lord of Guangye. Later, when the Han army was besieged, Li Shiqi urged the King of Han to seize Aocang's grain supplies and strategic positions. He then volunteered to persuade the King of Qi to submit to Han, successfully convincing Tian Guang to surrender. However, Han Xin attacked Qi anyway, and Tian Guang, believing Li Shiqi had deceived him, executed him.
Lu Jia of Chu was a skilled orator who served as an envoy for Emperor Gaozu. He was sent to South Vietnam to grant Wei Tuo the king's seal. When Wei Tuo received him disrespectfully, Lu Jia warned him that the Han emperor could easily destroy him. Wei Tuo apologized and acknowledged Han's superiority. Lu Jia successfully secured South Vietnam's submission. Later, when Emperor Gaozu dismissed the value of studying the classics, Lu Jia argued that while one could conquer the world on horseback, one could not govern it that way. He wrote twelve essays explaining why Qin fell and Han succeeded, which became known as the "New Speeches." During Empress Dowager Lu's regency, Lu Jia retired but later advised Chancellor Chen Ping to ally with General Zhou Bo to counter the Lu family's conspiracy. His strategy helped preserve the Liu imperial house.
Zhu Jian of Chu served as prime minister to Yingbu, King of Huainan, and advised against rebellion. After Yingbu rebelled and was suppressed, Zhu Jian was rewarded. He was known for his integrity and refused to associate with the corrupt Marquis of Piyang, who was favored by Empress Dowager Lu. When Zhu Jian's mother died, Lu Jia advised the Marquis of Piyang to offer generous funeral gifts, which led to reconciliation. Later, when the Marquis of Piyang was imprisoned, Zhu Jian secretly instructed the emperor's favorite minister to plead for his release, saving his life. After Empress Dowager Lu's death, Zhu Jian's earlier advice helped protect the Marquis of Piyang from execution. During Emperor Xiaowen's reign, Zhu Jian was implicated in a case involving the Marquis of Piyang and committed suicide to protect his family.
Lou Jing of Qi advised Emperor Gaozu to establish the capital in Guanzhong rather than Luoyang, arguing that Qin's former territory had natural defenses and abundant resources. Despite opposition from ministers from Shandong, Zhang Liang supported this plan, and the emperor adopted it, granting Lou Jing the surname Liu and the title of Feng Chunjun. Later, when the emperor planned to attack the Xiongnu, Lou Jing warned that the Xiongnu were deliberately showing weakness to ambush the Han army. The emperor ignored this advice, was besieged at Baideng, and later released Lou Jing, rewarding him. Lou Jing then proposed a marriage alliance with the Xiongnu, suggesting the emperor send his eldest princess to marry the Chanyu. Although Empress Lu objected, a substitute princess was sent. Lou Jing also recommended relocating powerful clans from various states to Guanzhong to strengthen the region.
Shusun Tong of Xue served under Qin II, cleverly avoiding punishment by calling rebels mere thieves. He later served Xiang Liang, King Huai, and finally surrendered to the King of Han. Noticing the disorderly behavior of ministers at court, he offered to create court rituals. Despite criticism from conservative Confucian scholars, he adapted ancient and Qin rituals to create a practical system. After the completion of Changle Palace, the new rituals were implemented, impressing Emperor Gaozu, who remarked, "Now I know the dignity of being emperor." Shusun Tong was appointed Fengchang and rewarded with gold, which he distributed to his disciples. He later served as Crown Prince Tutor and successfully dissuaded Emperor Gaozu from replacing the crown prince. Under Emperor Xiaohui, he continued to formulate rituals and established the practice of offering fruits at ancestral temples.

The evolution of religious and sacrificial practices during the Han Dynasty, focusing on the reigns of Emperors Wu, Zhao, Xuan, Yuan, Cheng, Ai, and Ping, as well as the usurper Wang Mang. The belief in ghosts and gods in Guangdong, where King Shuou’s reverence for them allegedly extended his life to 160 years, while neglect shortened his descendants’ lives. This led to the construction of temples and divination using chicken bones. Emperor Wu, influenced by alchemists like Gongsun Qing, built pavilions and towers in Chang’an and Ganquan Palace to invite immortals, including the Feilian, Gui, Yishou, and Longshou Pavilions, and the Tongtian Tower. He conducted sacrifices, such as those to Taiyi and Houtu, and expanded palace rooms. After a drought, Gongsun Qing cited the Yellow Emperor’s precedent, leading to a decree for worldwide worship of the spiritual star. Emperor Wu performed numerous rituals, including suburban sacrifices at Yongcheng, worship at Mount Tai, and construction of a Mingtang based on a Yellow Emperor-era design. He also built Jianzhang Palace, Taiye Pool with artificial islands, and the Shenming Terrace, all to attract gods. The calendar was revised, and the year was renamed Taichu. Alchemists continued to advise, leading to the construction of five cities and twelve towers. Emperor Wu made five pilgrimages to Mount Tai for sealing ceremonies, and sacrifices were made to various mountains and rivers.
During Emperor Zhao’s reign, he was too young to participate in sacrifices. Emperor Xuan honored Emperor Wu as Shizong, building temples where divine signs like white cranes and five-colored geese appeared. Emperor Xuan personally performed suburban sacrifices at Ganquan and Jiese, changing the era name to Sujue. He ordered annual sacrifices to the Yangtze River, sea, and Luoshui, and regular worship of the Five Mountains and Four Rivers. Alchemists advised building temples for various gods, including Suihou and Zhoukangbaoding. Doctor Liu Gengsheng was punished for failed alchemy. Jingzhao Yin Zhang Chang advised against alchemists, and many were dismissed. A tripod found in Meiyang was debated; Zhang Chang argued it was a Zhou dynasty artifact, not suitable for the ancestral temple. Phoenixes and other auspicious signs led to the construction of Bushou Palace and Phoenix Hall. Emperor Xuan died after a reign marked by frequent sacrifices and omens.
Emperor Yuan followed old rituals, performing suburban sacrifices every other year, but favored Confucianism. Ministers like Gong Yu and Wei Xuancheng proposed abolishing many temples, but Emperor Yuan reversed this after dreaming of divine condemnation. Emperor Cheng’s reign saw a major reform: Prime Minister Kuang Heng and Imperial Censor Zhang Tan argued that sacrifices should be moved to Chang’an’s northern and southern suburbs, citing ancient practices and the hardships of traveling to Ganquan and Fenyin. After debate, the move was approved, and many temples were abolished. However, after Emperor Cheng had no heirs, the Empress Dowager ordered the restoration of the old temples at Ganquan, Fenyin, and Yongcheng, blaming the move for the lack of descendants. Emperor Cheng later became obsessed with alchemists, but Gu Yong warned against them, citing historical failures. Du Ye also criticized the distant sacrifices. After Emperor Cheng’s death, the Empress Dowager restored the northern and southern suburbs.
Emperor Ai, ill, revived many temples, but after his death, the Empress Dowager again restored the Ganquan and Fenyin temples. Under Emperor Ping, Wang Mang reported extensively on sacrificial history, arguing for a return to the northern and southern suburbs and proposing a system where heaven and earth were worshiped together with ancestors. He established altars for the Five Emperors and various gods in Chang’an’s suburbs, and later added an official shrine for the god of grain. After usurping the throne, Wang Mang built the Eight Winds Tower and engaged in alchemy, with over 1,700 temples by his death. The text concludes with a commentary on the Han Dynasty’s ritual evolution, noting debates over the five virtues and the influence of alchemists, with Gu Yong’s criticisms deemed correct.

By consuming what was produced, expenses could be met, but hunger arose when grain was hoarded. A town of ten thousand households should have a collection of ten thousand bells and millions of strings of money. The government used money to buy titles and exempt people from punishment, leading to official chaos. Emperor Yuan of Han, son of Emperor Xuan, was made prince at age eight. He was generous and respected Confucianism, often criticizing his father's reliance on legal officials and harsh punishments. Emperor Xuan warned that Confucian scholars would disrupt the Han dynasty's system, which blended kingly and hegemonic rule. Though Emperor Xuan favored another son, he ultimately kept Emperor Yuan as heir due to loyalty to his mother.
Upon ascending the throne in 48 BCE, Emperor Yuan honored his mother and wife as empresses, granted amnesty, and distributed rewards. He issued edicts addressing natural disasters, earthquakes, and famines, ordering relief efforts, tax exemptions, and land grants to the poor. He reduced palace expenses, dismissed entertainers, and lent public lands to farmers. He also sent officials to inspect local governance and seek wise men. In subsequent years, Emperor Yuan continued responding to crises: earthquakes, floods, plagues, and famines led to further tax exemptions, amnesties, and relief measures. He abolished certain laws, reduced palace staff, and encouraged remonstrance. He appointed Confucian scholars like Gong Yu and Kuang Heng as officials, but his indecisiveness weakened the state. He also dealt with rebellions, such as the Xiqiang uprising, and military campaigns against the Xiongnu, including the execution of Zhizhi Chanyu.
Emperor Yuan's reign saw numerous natural disasters and social unrest. He repeatedly issued edicts blaming himself for poor governance and seeking advice. He reformed policies, including abolishing the death penalty for certain family crimes and reducing corvée labor. He also established his own mausoleum, Weiling, and ordered that no new migrants be forced to settle there.
Emperor Yuan died in 33 BCE after 16 years of rule. Ban Gu's commentary notes that Emperor Yuan was talented in music and calligraphy, respected Confucianism, and appointed many Confucian scholars as officials. However, his indecisiveness and adherence to literary principles led to the decline of Emperor Xuan's achievements. Despite this, his generosity, thrift, and gentle edicts reflected the legacy of ancient wise kings.

Emperor Hui of the Han Dynasty, son of Emperor Gaozu and Empress Lu, became crown prince in the second year of Gaozu's reign. After Gaozu's death in April of the twelfth year, Hui ascended the throne on May 17, with his mother becoming empress dowager. He issued decrees rewarding subjects with titles and promoting officials based on service length: Zhonglang and Langzhong officials serving six years received third-level promotions, those serving four years received second-level promotions, and various other officials received specific rewards. Those who organized Gaozu's funeral received monetary rewards based on salary, and those who built his mausoleum received gold. Land rent was reduced to one tax per fifteen people. Certain officials and their families were exempted from corvée labor except military tax. Princes were ordered to build Gaozu's ancestral temple.
In the first year of his reign, King Liu Ruyi of Zhao died. Subjects could atone for capital crimes with money. Commoners received title promotions. Chang'an city construction began. In the second year, King Hui of Qi presented Chengyang County to increase Princess Lu Yuan's territory. Two dragons appeared in Lanling, an earthquake struck Longxi, drought occurred, and Yanghou Liu Zhong and Prime Minister Xiao He died. In the third year, 146,000 workers built Chang'an for thirty days. A Liu family princess married the Xiongnu Shanyu. The King of Minyue was titled King of East China Sea, and 20,000 princes and slaves built Chang'an. A fire broke out in royal stables, and Zhao Tuo of South Vietnam paid tribute. In the fourth year, Zhang Ao's daughter became queen. Filial and loyal sages were exempted from corvée. The emperor held a crown ceremony with amnesty, abolished restrictive Qin laws, and fires occurred in Changle and Weiyang Palaces. In the fifth year, unusual weather included thunder and fruit blossoming in winter. Another 145,000 workers built Chang'an. Severe drought struck, Prime Minister Cao Shen died, and Chang'an city was completed. In the sixth year, King Fei of Qi died. Titles could be bought, and unmarried women aged fifteen to thirty were fined. Fan Kuai died, and the west city and Aocang were built. In the seventh year, chariot officers were sent to Xingyang. Solar eclipses occurred, and Emperor Hui died in Weiyang Palace on August 12, buried in Anling on September 5. Ban Gu commented that Hui was kind and respectful but fell short of saintliness due to Empress Lu's actions.

Empress Gao, of the Lu family, was the mother of Emperor Hui and assisted Emperor Gaozu in pacifying the realm. After Emperor Hui ascended, she became the Queen Mother. She arranged for her granddaughter, the daughter of Princess Lu Yuan, to be the Queen, who had no children, so a son from a harem beauty was made prince. Upon Emperor Hui's death, this prince became emperor, but due to his youth, Empress Dowager Lu ruled in his stead, granting amnesty and promoting her relatives: four of her brother's sons were made kings, and six others were made princes. In the first year of her reign, she abolished harsh laws and rewarded the people. She established officials to encourage filial piety. In the second year, she ordered merit rankings for princes to be preserved in the ancestral temple. Natural events occurred: earthquakes, solar eclipses, and floods. In the fourth year, the young emperor, aware he was not the Queen's biological son, complained and was imprisoned. The Empress Dowager replaced him with Liu Hong, King of Hengshan. In the fifth year, Wei Tuo, King of Nanyue, declared himself emperor. In the sixth year, there was a general amnesty and construction at Changling. The Xiongnu invaded in the seventh year, and several kings died or were imprisoned. In the eighth year, Empress Lu died in Weiyang Palace.
After her death, Lu Lu and Lu Chan, holding military and political power, plotted rebellion. Zhu Xuhou Liu Zhang, son of King Qi, learned of this and coordinated with his brother, King Qi, and officials Zhou Bo and Chen Ping to counter them. King Qi raised an army, and General Guan Ying, sent to stop him, instead allied with him. Zhou Bo, using deception, gained control of the Northern Army by tricking Lu Lu into surrendering his command. Lu Chan, attempting a coup, was killed by Liu Zhang. The Lu family was then exterminated. The ministers, believing the young emperor and his brothers were not Emperor Hui's sons, killed them and enthroned Emperor Wen. Ban Gu noted that under Empress Gao, the world was peaceful, with reduced warfare and punishments, allowing the people to prosper in farming.
